rabat.s: Rabat is a city on the Atlantic coast of Morocco, now the country's capital. Under the Almohad Caliphate it was developed as a fortified military base.

rabih-az-zubayr.s: Rabih az-Zubayr was a Sudanese warlord and slave trader who built a powerful state in the Lake Chad region in the late nineteenth century. He conquered Bornu in 1893 and threatened Wadai.

rabihs-conquest-of-bornu.s: Rabih's conquest of Bornu was the seizure of the kingdom of Bornu, the successor of the Kanem-Bornu Empire, by the Sudanese warlord Rabih az-Zubayr in 1893. It overthrew the old ruling order west of Lake Chad.

racial-segregation.s: Racial segregation is the enforced separation of people of different races in housing, public life and rights. The Italian Empire codified racial segregation in its African colonies through a series of laws, particularly after the conquest of Ethiopia.

raden-wijaya.s: Raden Wijaya was the founder and first ruler of the Majapahit Empire in eastern Java, reigning from 1293 to 1309 CE. He used a Mongol expedition sent by Kublai Khan of the Yuan Dynasty to defeat his rivals, then turned against the Mongol forces and drove them out.

raffia-cloth.s: Raffia cloth is a textile woven from the fibres of the raffia palm, produced in Central Africa. In the Kingdom of Kongo it was a valuable good and also served as a form of currency.

ragamuffin-war.s: The Ragamuffin War, or Farroupilha, was a republican and separatist revolt in the southern Brazilian province of Rio Grande do Sul, lasting from 1835 to 1845. It was the longest of the provincial rebellions that shook the Brazilian Empire during and after the Regency period.

raigad.s: Raigad is a hill fort in the Western Ghats of Maharashtra, India. It was one of the strategic forts controlled by Shivaji and became his capital.

rajapur.s: Rajapur is a port town on the Konkan coast of Maharashtra, western India. Under the Maratha Empire it was one of the ports, alongside Dabhol, through which maritime trade linked the Deccan to the Arabian Sea.

rajendra-chola-i.s: Rajendra Chola I was an emperor of the Chola dynasty of southern India in the early eleventh century. In 1025 he launched a major naval expedition against the Srivijaya Empire, raiding its ports.

rajgad.s: Rajgad is a hill fort in the Sahyadri range near Pune in Maharashtra. It was one of the key forts secured by Shivaji in building his power in the Western Ghats.

rajputs.s: The Rajputs are a group of warrior clans of northern and western India, many of whom ruled kingdoms in Rajasthan and neighbouring regions. They resisted the Delhi Sultanate and the early Mughal Empire, as at the Battle of Khanwa against Babur in 1527, but many later became…

ramadan.s: Ramadan is the ninth month of the Islamic calendar, observed by Muslims as a month of fasting, prayer and reflection. According to the Almohad Caliphate profile, it was towards the end of Ramadan in 1121 that Ibn Tumart proclaimed himself the Mahdi.

ramesses-ii.s: Ramesses II was a pharaoh of the Nineteenth Dynasty of the Egyptian New Kingdom, who reigned for much of the thirteenth century BCE. He fought the Hittite king Muwatalli II at the Battle of Kadesh in 1274 BCE and later concluded a peace treaty with the Hittite Empire.

ramesses-iii.s: Ramesses III was a pharaoh of the Twentieth Dynasty of the Egyptian New Kingdom. He defeated land and sea invasions by the Sea Peoples around 1177 BCE, preserving Egypt during the Late Bronze Age collapse.

ramesses-xi.s: Ramesses XI was the last pharaoh of the Twentieth Dynasty and of the Egyptian New Kingdom. During his reign real power passed to the high priests of Amun in Thebes and to military commanders.

rampjaar.s: The Rampjaar, or disaster year, was 1672 in the history of the Dutch Republic. France under Louis XIV invaded with a vast army while England attacked by sea, and the republic was nearly overrun.

rangaku.s: Rangaku, meaning Dutch learning, was the body of European scientific and technical knowledge studied in Japan through the Dutch trading post at Dejima. During the Tokugawa Shogunate's period of restricted foreign contact, Japanese scholars translated and analysed European…

ranjit-singh.s: Ranjit Singh was the founder and Maharaja of the Sikh Empire, who lived from 1780 to 1839. Born into the Sukerchakia Misl, he seized Lahore in 1799 and united the Sikh confederacies of the Punjab under his rule.

ras.s: Ras, meaning head, was one of the highest noble and military titles in the Ethiopian Empire, below that of the negus. It was held by powerful regional lords and governors.

rashid-al-din-hamadani.s: Rashid al-Din Hamadani was a Persian physician, statesman and historian who served as vizier of the Ilkhanate. He carried out the extensive reforms of Ghazan Khan and wrote the Jami al-Tawarikh, a universal history of Eurasia.

rashidun-caliphate.s: The Rashidun Caliphate was the first Islamic caliphate, ruled by the four rightly guided caliphs Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali from the death of the Prophet Muhammad in 632 CE until 661 CE. It reunified Arabia in the Ridda Wars and conquered the Sasanian Empire and the…

rastafari.s: Rastafari is a religious and cultural movement that emerged in Jamaica in the 1930s. It regards Emperor Haile Selassie of Ethiopia as a messianic figure.

ravi.s: The Ravi is one of the five rivers of the Punjab, flowing from the Himalayas through India and Pakistan, with Lahore on its banks. With the Jhelum, Chenab, Beas and Sutlej, it sustained intensive cultivation of wheat, cotton and sugarcane.

rayy.s: Rayy was an ancient city in northern Iran, near modern Tehran, and a major centre on the Silk Road. Under the Seljuk Empire it was one of the cities, alongside Nishapur and Isfahan, from which sultans drew substantial revenue by taxing caravan traffic.

reconquista.s: The Reconquista refers to the centuries-long series of campaigns by Christian kingdoms of the Iberian Peninsula to conquer the territories ruled by Muslims, completed with the fall of Granada in 1492. The Almoravid Empire and the Almohad Caliphate intervened in al-Andalus to…

recopilacion-de-leyes-de-los-reinos-de-l.n: Recopilación de Leyes de los Reinos de las Indias
recopilacion-de-leyes-de-los-reinos-de-l.s: The Recopilación de Leyes de los Reinos de las Indias was a comprehensive compilation of the laws governing Spain's American territories, published in 1680. It was produced under the Council of the Indies, which governed the colonies from Madrid.

red-sea.s: The Red Sea is a narrow arm of the Indian Ocean between north-east Africa and the Arabian Peninsula, connected to the Mediterranean by the Suez isthmus. It has long been a major trade route between the Mediterranean, Arabia, India and East Africa.

red-turban-rebellion.s: The Red Turban Rebellion was a series of uprisings against Mongol rule in China, beginning in 1351 under the influence of White Lotus millenarian beliefs and lasting to 1368. It spread across central China and produced competing warlords.

regency-period-brazil.s: The Regency period was the era from 1831 to 1840 when Brazil was governed by regents on behalf of the young Pedro II after his father's abdication. It was marked by serial provincial rebellions, including the Cabanagem and the Ragamuffin War.

regional-autonomy-and-warlordism.s: Regional autonomy and warlordism are a recurring cause of imperial decline, as provincial governors, generals or local lords accumulate independent military and fiscal power and cease to obey the centre. The process fragments the state and often leads to civil war.

reichsrat.s: The Reichsrat was the parliament of the Austrian half of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, sitting in Vienna. Under the 1867 Compromise it governed the Austrian lands, while the Hungarian Diet in Budapest governed the Hungarian half.

reichstag.s: The Reichstag was the national parliament of the German Empire, elected by universal male suffrage. It voted on legislation and the budget but could not appoint or remove ministers, who were responsible to the Kaiser alone.

reinsurance-treaty.s: The Reinsurance Treaty was a secret agreement between the German Empire and Russia, concluded by Bismarck in 1887, in which each promised neutrality in most wars involving the other. After Bismarck's dismissal it was allowed to lapse in 1890.

reliance-on-mercenaries.s: Reliance on mercenaries is a recurring structural feature of empires that hire foreign or professional soldiers instead of relying on citizen or subject levies. Mercenaries can provide skilled forces quickly but are costly and may mutiny or change sides when pay fails.

religious-legitimacy.s: Religious legitimacy is a recurring source of imperial strength, as rulers claim divine sanction or a sacred role to justify their authority and command loyalty. It can take the form of divine kingship, a caliphal title or a ruler's link to sacred institutions.

religious-persecution-and-sectarian-stri.s: Religious persecution and sectarian strife are a recurring cause of imperial weakness, as conflict between faiths or within a faith alienates subjects and divides elites. Rulers who impose religious uniformity may provoke revolt or lose productive communities.

religious-pluralism.s: Religious pluralism is the coexistence of several religions within a single society or state. The Khazar Khaganate was notable for accommodating Judaism, Christianity, Islam and traditional beliefs, which eased commercial relations with diverse partners.

religious-tolerance.s: Religious tolerance is the acceptance by a state of religious beliefs and practices different from those of its rulers. The Achaemenid Empire under Cyrus the Great allowed deported peoples to return and rebuild their temples, as recorded on the Cyrus Cylinder.

renaissance.s: The Renaissance was a period of cultural revival in Europe from the fourteenth to the sixteenth century, beginning in Italy and centred on the recovery of classical learning. It drew on Greek texts and scholars from the Byzantine Empire, on Arabic science from the Abbasid…

renaissance-of-the-12th-century.s: The Renaissance of the 12th century was a period of intellectual revival in western Europe marked by the recovery of Greek and Arabic learning, the growth of cathedral schools and the rise of the first universities. It built on the classical Latin texts preserved and copied…

repatriation-of-cultural-property.s: Repatriation of cultural property refers to the return of artworks and artefacts removed from their countries or communities of origin, often through conquest or colonial looting. The Benin Bronzes, some 3,000 works taken by British forces from the Benin Empire in 1897, are…

republic-of-turkey.s: The Republic of Turkey is the modern state founded in Anatolia after the dissolution of the Ottoman Empire following the First World War. Established under the leadership of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, it replaced the sultanate and caliphate with a secular, nationalist republic…

republican-party-brazil.s: The Republican Party of Brazil was a political movement founded in 1869 that campaigned for the replacement of the monarchy with a republic. Growing steadily through the 1880s, it attracted much of the landowning elite of São Paulo and offered an organised political…

republicanism.s: Republicanism refers to the political idea that the state should be a public matter governed by citizens or their representatives rather than by a hereditary monarch. It shaped the founding traditions of the Roman Republic that preceded the Roman Empire and resurfaced…

reservoir.s: A reservoir is an artificial or enlarged body of water used to store water for irrigation, drinking or flood control. In the Khmer Empire, vast reservoirs known as barays, together with canals and embankments, formed one of the most sophisticated hydraulic systems of the…

revolt-of-cyrus-the-younger.s: The Revolt of Cyrus the Younger was a rebellion in 401 BCE in which a Persian prince hired Greek mercenaries to seize the throne from his brother Artaxerxes II. Cyrus was killed at the Battle of Cunaxa, and the retreat of the surviving Greek force was recorded by Xenophon.

revolt-of-the-three-feudatories.s: The Revolt of the Three Feudatories was a rebellion in southern China between 1673 and 1681 led by powerful Chinese generals, among them Wu Sangui, who had been granted hereditary fiefdoms for helping the Qing conquest. When the Kangxi Emperor moved to abolish these fiefdoms,…

revolts-of-522-520-bce.s: The revolts of 522–520 BCE were a wave of rebellions that broke out across the Achaemenid Empire during the disputed succession that brought Darius I to the throne. Darius suppressed them in a series of campaigns later commemorated in the Behistun Inscription.

reza-abbasi.s: Reza Abbasi was a leading Persian painter and calligrapher active at the court of the Safavid ruler Shah Abbas I in Isfahan. He is celebrated for single-figure studies and graceful line drawings that influenced later Persian painting.

reza-qoli.s: Reza Qoli was the eldest son of Nader Shah, founder of the Afsharid Empire, and served for a time as a regent and commander. In 1741 Nader had him blinded on suspicion of involvement in a conspiracy against his life.

rhine.s: The Rhine is a major river of western Europe that flows from the Alps to the North Sea. Under the Carolingian Empire it served, with the Danube, as a principal commercial artery, and the Saxon Wars were fought against peoples living east of it.

rhinoplasty.s: Rhinoplasty is surgery to reconstruct or reshape the nose. Early descriptions of the procedure appear in the surgical compendium attributed to the Indian physician Sushruta.

rhodes.s: Rhodes is an island in the south-eastern Aegean Sea, off the coast of Anatolia, long valued as a naval and commercial base. In the seventh century it became a target of the first Arab fleets built under Muawiyah as governor of Syria.

ribat.s: A ribat was a fortified religious community or frontier stronghold in the Islamic world, combining military defence with devotion and study. The Almoravid movement grew from a ribat founded by the preacher Abd Allah ibn Yasin among the Lamtuna Berbers.

rice.s: Rice is a cereal grain cultivated in flooded paddies or dry fields and is a staple food across much of Asia and parts of West Africa. It underpinned the economies of many empires, including the Han, Song and Ming dynasties of China, the Khmer and Majapahit empires of Southeast…

rice-terrace.s: A rice terrace is a series of stepped, levelled fields cut into hillsides to allow the irrigated cultivation of rice on sloping ground. Terracing conserves water and soil and makes intensive farming possible in upland areas.

richard-i-of-england.s: Richard I of England, known as Richard the Lionheart, was King of England from 1189 to 1199 and a leading commander of the Third Crusade. He fought Saladin's forces in the Levant, taking part in the capture of Acre and winning victories on the coast, but did not retake Jerusalem.

ridda-wars.s: The Ridda Wars, or Wars of Apostasy, were a series of campaigns fought in 632–633 CE by the first caliph, Abu Bakr, against Arabian tribes that broke away after the death of the Prophet Muhammad. Many tribes rallied around rival prophetic claimants such as Musaylima and Sajah.

riksdag.s: The Riksdag is the national assembly of Sweden, whose origins lie in the late medieval and early modern period. During the era of the Swedish Empire it brought together representatives of the realm to approve taxation, levies and major decisions of state.

riksdag-of-the-estates.s: The Riksdag of the Estates was the form of the Swedish parliament in which representatives sat in four separate estates: the nobility, the clergy, the burghers and the peasantry. Its inclusion of a peasant estate was unusual among European assemblies of the time.

rim-sin-i.s: Rim-Sin I was a long-reigning king of Larsa in southern Mesopotamia and one of the most powerful rulers of the region in the early second millennium BCE. A contemporary letter quoted in accounts of the Babylonian Empire name him alongside Hammurabi as one of several kings of…

rim-sin-ii.s: Rim-Sin II was a pretender who led a widespread rebellion of southern Mesopotamian cities against Babylon shortly after the death of Hammurabi. According to the Babylonian Empire profile, the revolt spread across 26 southern cities and was crushed by Hammurabi's son Samsu-iluna.

rimush.s: Rimush was a king of the Akkadian Empire and a son and successor of Sargon of Akkad. His reign was dominated by campaigns to suppress revolts among the Sumerian cities and other subject territories.

ringstrasse.s: The Ringstrasse is a grand circular boulevard in Vienna built in the second half of the nineteenth century on the site of the demolished city walls. It was lined with major public buildings, including parliament, the opera, museums and the university, as well as private…

rinji.s: Rinji was the Hausa term for slave villages or plantation settlements attached to the estates of emirs, officials and wealthy merchants in the Sokoto Caliphate. Enslaved people living in them produced grain and other crops for their owners.

rio-de-janeiro.s: Rio de Janeiro is a major port city on the south-eastern coast of Brazil. It became the seat of the Portuguese court in 1808 and then served as the capital of the Brazilian Empire throughout its existence.

rio-de-la-plata.s: The Río de la Plata is the broad estuary formed by the Paraná and Uruguay rivers on the border of modern Argentina and Uruguay, and by extension the surrounding region. Control of its eastern bank was contested between Portuguese Brazil and Spanish, later Argentine, authorities.

rio-grande-do-sul.s: Rio Grande do Sul is the southernmost province, now a state, of Brazil, bordering Uruguay and Argentina. During the Brazilian Empire it was the scene of the Farroupilha or Ragamuffin War of 1835–1845, in which republican separatists maintained an independent republic for…

roads-and-communication-networks.s: Roads and communication networks refers to the recurring pattern in which empires built routes, relay stations and postal systems to move armies, officials, information and goods across large territories. Such networks allowed central governments to collect taxes, respond to…

robert-sherley.s: Robert Sherley was an English adventurer who, with his brother Anthony, travelled to the court of the Safavid ruler Shah Abbas I at the end of the sixteenth century. He later served the shah as an envoy to European courts.

rock-hewn-churches-of-lalibela.s: The rock-hewn churches of Lalibela are a group of medieval churches carved directly out of rock in the town of Lalibela in the highlands of northern Ethiopia. They are traditionally associated with King Lalibela of the Zagwe dynasty and are a major site of Ethiopian Orthodox…

rokosz.s: Rokosz was the legally recognised right of the Polish nobility to form a confederation in armed rebellion against a king believed to have violated his obligations. It was grounded in the conditions the nobility imposed on elected monarchs, including the Henrician Articles of…

roman-annexation-of-egypt.s: The Roman annexation of Egypt took place in 30 BCE, when Octavian took Alexandria after the defeat of Mark Antony and Cleopatra VII. Following the deaths of Antony and Cleopatra, Egypt became a Roman province under the direct control of the emperor.

roman-annexation-of-syria.s: The Roman annexation of Syria took place in 63 BCE, when the Roman general Pompey deposed the last Seleucid rulers and organised Syria as a Roman province. By then the Seleucid state had been reduced to a small, divided remnant around Antioch.

roman-empire.s: The Roman Empire was the state ruled by emperors from Rome after the end of the Roman Republic, at its height controlling the entire Mediterranean world and much of western Europe and the Near East. Its western half ended with the deposition of Romulus Augustulus in 476 CE,…

roman-expedition-against-the-garamantes-.n: Roman expedition against the Garamantes (19 BCE)
roman-expedition-against-the-garamantes-.s: The Roman expedition against the Garamantes was a punitive campaign led in 19 BCE by Lucius Cornelius Balbus, the proconsul of Africa, into the Fezzan region of the central Sahara. According to the Garamantian Empire profile, Balbus captured fifteen Garamantian settlements,…

roman-law.s: Roman law is the legal system developed in ancient Rome from the Twelve Tables through centuries of statutes, magistrates' edicts and the writings of jurists. It was systematised in the sixth century under the Byzantine emperor Justinian in the Corpus Juris Civilis.

roman-republic.s: The Roman Republic was the system of government of ancient Rome from the expulsion of the kings, traditionally dated to 509 BCE, until the rise of Augustus in the late first century BCE. Governed by elected magistrates and the Senate, it expanded across Italy and the…

roman-senate.s: The Roman Senate was the governing council of ancient Rome, composed largely of former magistrates and members of leading families. Under the Roman Republic it directed foreign policy, finance and war, while under the emperors its authority became largely formal.

roman-triumph.s: The Roman triumph was a ceremonial procession through Rome granted to a victorious general, in which he paraded with his troops, captives and spoils. Under the emperors the honour was increasingly reserved for members of the imperial family.

romania.s: Romania is a country in south-eastern Europe, formed in the nineteenth century from the union of the principalities of Wallachia and Moldavia. After the First World War it was greatly enlarged with territories, including Transylvania, taken from the dissolved Austro-Hungarian…

romanians.s: Romanians are a people of south-eastern Europe who speak a Romance language derived from Latin. Within the Austro-Hungarian Empire, large Romanian communities lived in Transylvania and other eastern regions under Hungarian administration.

romanos-iv-diogenes.s: Romanos IV Diogenes was a Byzantine emperor who reigned from 1068 to 1071. He led a major campaign against the Seljuk Turks and was defeated and captured by Sultan Alp Arslan at the Battle of Manzikert in 1071.

romanticism.s: Romanticism was a cultural and intellectual movement of the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries that emphasised emotion, imagination, the past and national identity. In Poland it was closely bound up with the loss of statehood after the partitions.

romanus-pontifex.s: Romanus Pontifex is a papal bull, one of a series of fifteenth-century papal documents that granted Iberian crowns rights over newly encountered lands and peoples outside Christendom. Accounts of the Spanish Empire cite it, together with Inter Caetera and the Treaty of…

rome.s: Rome is a city in central Italy that grew from a small settlement on the Tiber into the capital of the Roman Republic and Roman Empire, and later the seat of the papacy. As the centre of Roman power it fought Carthage, conquered the Seleucid, Ptolemaic and Macedonian kingdoms…

romulus-augustulus.s: Romulus Augustulus was the last emperor of the Western Roman Empire, a youth placed on the throne by his father, the general Orestes. He was deposed in 476 CE by the Germanic commander Odoacer, a date conventionally used to mark the end of Roman rule in the West.

rostam-farrokhzad.s: Rostam Farrokhzad was a Sasanian Persian general and leading figure at the court in the final years of the Sasanian Empire. He commanded the Persian army at the Battle of al-Qadisiyyah, where he was defeated and killed by Arab Muslim forces under Saad ibn Abi Waqqas.

round-city-of-baghdad.s: The Round City of Baghdad, officially named Madinat al-Salam or the City of Peace, was the circular walled capital founded in 762 by the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur on the Tigris. Its concentric walls enclosed the caliphal palace and great mosque at the centre, with gates facing…

rouran-khaganate.s: The Rouran Khaganate was a nomadic confederation that dominated the Mongolian steppe from the late fourth to the mid-sixth century CE. The Göktürks under Bumin of the Ashina clan were originally its vassals, and their revolt destroyed Rouran power in the 550s.

royal-navy.s: The Royal Navy is the naval service of Britain, which developed from the English navy into the most powerful fleet in the world between the eighteenth and early twentieth centuries. It protected trade routes, defended the British Isles and projected power to colonies across…

royal-niger-company.s: The Royal Niger Company was a British chartered company that held a commercial monopoly and administrative powers over territories along the lower Niger in the 1880s and 1890s. Its charter was revoked in 1900, when its territories passed to the British government and became…

royal-road.s: The Royal Road was an ancient highway of the Achaemenid Empire running about 2,700 kilometres from Susa to Sardis, with relay stations along its length. Royal couriers using fresh horses could carry messages across it in around seven days.

rozvi-empire.s: The Rozvi Empire was a state on the Zimbabwean plateau that emerged in the late seventeenth century under the Changamire dynasty, after breaking away from and overshadowing the Mutapa state. Its economy rested on cattle-based patronage, the gold and ivory trade and tribute…

rubattino-shipping-company.s: The Rubattino shipping company was a Genoese steamship company that purchased land at Assab Bay on the Red Sea coast in 1869. In 1882 the Italian government assumed control of the site.

rubber.s: Rubber is an elastic material produced from the latex of certain tropical trees, which became an important industrial commodity in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries with the growth of bicycles, automobiles and electrical industries. Colonial powers established…

rule-of-law.s: The rule of law is the principle that all people and institutions, including governments, are subject to and accountable under publicly known laws applied equally. It is closely associated with British constitutional traditions.

rupee.s: The rupee is a currency unit of the Indian subcontinent, descended from the silver rupiya coin introduced in the sixteenth century and later standardised under Mughal rule. It remained the main unit of account in South Asia into the colonial and modern periods.

rupiya.s: The rupiya was a silver coin introduced in northern India in the sixteenth century under Sher Shah Suri and adopted as the standard silver coinage of the Mughal Empire. Its consistent weight and purity made it widely trusted in trade.

russia.s: Russia is a vast country spanning eastern Europe and northern Asia, which grew from the principality of Moscow into the Russian Empire and later the Soviet Union. As a major power it fought repeatedly against the Swedish Empire, the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth and the…

russian-empire.s: The Russian Empire was the state ruled by the Romanov dynasty from Peter the Great's proclamation of the empire in 1721 until the revolution of 1917. It expanded across eastern Europe, the Caucasus, Central Asia and Siberia to become one of the largest empires in history.

russian-judicial-reform-of-1864.s: The Russian judicial reform of 1864 was one of the Great Reforms of Tsar Alexander II, which reorganised the courts of the Russian Empire. It introduced public trials, trial by jury for serious criminal cases, independent judges, an organised legal profession and justices of…

russian-orthodox-church.s: The Russian Orthodox Church is the branch of Eastern Orthodox Christianity that developed after the conversion of Kievan Rus in the late tenth century. It became closely tied to Muscovite and then Russian imperial authority, and Peter the Great placed it under state control by…

russian-revolution-of-1905.s: The Russian Revolution of 1905 was a wave of strikes, peasant uprisings, mutinies and political protest across the Russian Empire, sparked by the Bloody Sunday massacre in Saint Petersburg and defeat in the war with Japan. It forced Tsar Nicholas II to issue the October…

russo-japanese-war.s: The Russo-Japanese War was a conflict between the Russian Empire and the Empire of Japan over influence in Manchuria and Korea, concluded by the Treaty of Portsmouth in 1905. Japan won decisive victories on land and at sea, including the destruction of the Russian fleet at…

russo-turkish-war-1768-1774.s: The Russo-Turkish War of 1768–1774 was a conflict between the Russian Empire under Catherine the Great and the Ottoman Empire. Russian forces won major victories on land and at sea, and the Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca ended the war by granting Russia access to the Black Sea and…

russo-turkish-war-1877-1878.s: The Russo-Turkish War of 1877–1878 was fought between the Russian Empire and the Ottoman Empire, following uprisings among the Balkan Christian peoples. Russia's victory led to the Treaty of San Stefano and then the Congress of Berlin in 1878, which recognised the independence…

rye.s: Rye is a hardy cereal grain that grows well in cool climates and poorer soils, long a staple of northern and eastern European agriculture. The Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth exported large quantities of rye and wheat through the Baltic port of Gdańsk to the Netherlands,…

red-army.s: The Red Army was the army of Soviet Russia and then the Soviet Union, founded by the Bolsheviks in 1918 under Leon Trotsky to fight the Russian Civil War. It conquered the independent republics of the Caucasus, Central Asia and Ukraine in 1920–1921 and later drove the German…

rewa-kantha-agency.s: The Rewa Kantha Agency was a British political agency in eastern Gujarat that supervised the princely states along the Narmada, called Rewa in Gujarati, and the Mahi, among them Rajpipla, Chhota Udaipur, Baria and Lunavada, together with many small chiefships. After…

rio-grande.s: The Rio Grande is a river that rises in Colorado and flows south through New Mexico, then forms the border between Texas and Mexico to the Gulf of Mexico. Its upper valley was the heart of Pueblo country and of Spanish New Mexico.

roger-ii-of-sicily.s: Roger II was Count of Sicily from 1105, then united the Norman lands of southern Italy by taking Apulia and Calabria, Capua, Bari and Naples. He was crowned the first king of Sicily in 1130.

red-river-asia.s: The Red River rises in Yunnan in China and flows south-east through northern Vietnam to the Gulf of Tonkin. Its fertile, flood-prone delta, where Hanoi stands, was the heartland of the earliest Vietnamese states and of later dynasties, which built great dikes to control it.

rene-of-anjou.s: René of Anjou was Duke of Anjou, Count of Provence and Duke of Bar, and by marriage Duke of Lorraine, as well as titular king of Naples, Sicily and Jerusalem. He lost Naples to Alfonso of Aragon in 1442.

rudolf-i-of-germany.s: Rudolf I of Germany, a Swabian count of the Habsburg family, was elected King of the Romans in 1273, ending the Great Interregnum after the fall of the Hohenstaufen. He defeated Ottokar II of Bohemia in 1278 and gave Austria and Styria to his sons, founding Habsburg power there.

rudolf-iii-of-burgundy.s: Rudolf III was the last king of the Kingdom of Burgundy, also called Arles, reigning from 993 to 1032. Weak against his nobles, he relied on bishops, granting the bishop of Lausanne the county of Vaud in 1011.

ran-min.s: Ran Min was a Han Chinese general of the Later Zhao, adopted into its ruling Shi family. After the death of Shi Hu he seized power in 350, ordered the killing of the Jie and other non-Chinese at Ye, and proclaimed the state of Wei, known as Ran Wei.

republic-of-new-granada.s: The Republic of New Granada was the state formed by present-day Colombia and Panama after the break-up of Gran Colombia in 1830–1831. Its government at Bogotá faced the War of the Supremes of 1839–1842, a civil war of regional leaders during which Panama briefly broke away as…

rafael-carrera.s: Rafael Carrera was a Guatemalan caudillo of humble origins who in 1837 led a peasant revolt against the liberal government of the Federal Republic of Central America. His victory helped break up the federation, and he dominated Guatemala from 1839, intervening in El Salvador…

rajputana-agency.s: The Rajputana Agency was the British political office that supervised the princely states of Rajputana in north-western India, under an agent to the Governor-General based at Mount Abu. The states kept their own rulers under treaties with the British but accepted British…

ramon-berenguer-iv-count-of-barcelona.n: Ramon Berenguer IV, Count of Barcelona
ramon-berenguer-iv-count-of-barcelona.s: Ramon Berenguer IV was Count of Barcelona from 1131. His betrothal in 1137 to Petronilla, heiress of Aragon, joined Aragon and Catalonia in the dynastic union later called the Crown of Aragon.

rhine-province.s: The Rhine Province was a province of Prussia in western Germany, formed in 1822 from lands on both banks of the Rhine that Prussia gained at the Congress of Vienna, with Koblenz as its capital. It absorbed many former ecclesiastical states, imperial cities and small…

robert-guiscard.s: Robert Guiscard was a Norman adventurer of the Hauteville family who became Duke of Apulia and Calabria in 1059. He took Bari in 1071, ending Byzantine rule in southern Italy, and conquered Amalfi in 1073 and Salerno in 1076.

rama-i.s: Rama I, known before his accession as Chao Phraya Chakri, was a general of King Taksin of Thonburi who drove the Burmese from Lan Na and brought the Emerald Buddha from Vientiane in 1779. In 1782 he became king, founding the Chakri dynasty and the new capital at Bangkok, the…

records-of-the-grand-historian.s: The Records of the Grand Historian, or Shiji, is a history of China from the legendary Yellow Emperor to the reign of Emperor Wu of Han, completed by Sima Qian around 91 BCE on the work of his father Sima Tan. Its annals, tables, treatises and biographies became the model for…

reichsdeputationshauptschluss.s: The Reichsdeputationshauptschluss, or Imperial Recess, was the final resolution of an imperial deputation adopted at Regensburg in 1803. To compensate German princes for lands lost to France on the left bank of the Rhine, it secularised almost all church states and abolished…

rajatarangini.s: The Rajatarangini, the River of Kings, is a Sanskrit verse chronicle of the kings of Kashmir written by the poet Kalhana in 1148–1149. It traces the valley's rulers from legendary times to the 12th century, becoming more detailed and reliable for later periods, and is the main…

rafael-nunez.s: Rafael Núñez was a Colombian politician from Cartagena who served four times as president. Breaking with the radical liberals, he led the Regeneration movement and replaced the federal United States of Colombia with the centralised Republic of Colombia under the constitution…

raj-gond.s: The Raj Gonds are the ruling and landowning section of the Gond people of central India. Gond kingdoms such as Garha-Mandla, Deogarh and Chanda dominated the region from the 15th to the 18th century, and Raj Gond families held several smaller princely states in Chhattisgarh…

ramon-berenguer-iii-of-barcelona.s: Ramon Berenguer III, called the Great, was count of Barcelona from 1086 to 1131. He gained Besalú and Cerdanya by inheritance and, through his marriage to Douce in 1112, the County of Provence.

ranbir-singh-of-jammu-and-kashmir.n: Ranbir Singh of Jammu and Kashmir
ranbir-singh-of-jammu-and-kashmir.s: Ranbir Singh was the second Dogra maharaja of Jammu and Kashmir, succeeding his father Gulab Singh in 1857. He supported the British in 1857, extended control over Gilgit, and issued a law code known as the Ranbir Penal Code.

ranbir-singh-of-jind.s: Ranbir Singh was the last ruling maharaja of the Sikh princely state of Jind in the Punjab, reigning from 1887 to 1948. He sent troops to fight for Britain in the First World War and was rewarded with a higher gun salute.

red-guards-russia.s: The Red Guards were armed workers' militias formed in Russian cities in 1917 and controlled by the Bolsheviks. They helped seize power in the October Revolution and spread Soviet rule to Ukraine, the Black Sea coast and Central Asia, often with great violence, as at Kokand and…

regency-council-kingdom-of-poland.s: The Regency Council was the governing body of the Kingdom of Poland created by Germany and Austria-Hungary during the First World War. Formed in 1917 by Archbishop Aleksander Kakowski, Prince Zdzisław Lubomirski and Józef Ostrowski, it built up Polish administration, courts…

reza-shah.s: Reza Shah was an officer of the Persian Cossack Brigade who seized power in a coup in 1921 as Reza Khan. He became prime minister in 1923 and in 1925 the Majlis deposed the last Qajar shah and made him shah, founding the Pahlavi dynasty.

rhenish-hesse.s: Rhenish Hesse is a region on the left bank of the Rhine around Mainz and Worms, known for its vineyards. The Congress of Vienna settlement gave it to the Grand Duchy of Hesse in 1816 in exchange for Westphalia, and it remained one of Hesse's three provinces until 1945.

ruaidri-mac-duinn-sleibe.s: Ruaidrí Mac Duinn Sléibe was the last powerful king of Ulaid, the over-kingdom of eastern Ulster, and head of the Dál Fiatach. In 1177 the Anglo-Norman adventurer John de Courcy invaded and defeated him near Downpatrick, and despite repeated attempts he could not recover his…

russo-circassian-war.s: The Russo-Circassian War was the long struggle of the Circassian peoples of the north-western Caucasus against Russian conquest, usually dated from 1763 to 1864. Russian forts, raids and blockades wore down the Circassian principalities and tribes.

rafael-trujillo.s: Rafael Trujillo was dictator of the Dominican Republic from 1930 to 1961. He rose through the National Guard created during the US occupation and seized power in 1930.

rajasinha-ii-of-kandy.s: Rajasinha II was king of Kandy from 1635 to 1687. He invited the Dutch East India Company to help expel the Portuguese from Sri Lanka, signing a treaty in 1638, but the Dutch kept the captured coastal forts for themselves.

ralph-moor.s: Sir Ralph Moor was a British colonial administrator who served as commissioner of the Niger Coast Protectorate from 1896 and then as the first high commissioner of the Protectorate of Southern Nigeria from 1900 to 1903. He organised the punitive expedition of 1897 that sacked…

ramon-iii-of-pallars-jussa.s: Ramon III was the first count of Pallars Jussà. When his father Count Sunyer of Pallars died in 1011, the county was divided: Ramon received the lower lands around Tremp, while his brother Guillem took Pallars Sobirà.

rann-of-kutch.s: The Rann of Kutch is a vast seasonal salt marsh in western India and south-eastern Pakistan, divided into the Great Rann and the Little Rann. Flooded in the monsoon and a white salt desert in the dry season, it separated Kutch from mainland Gujarat, and small chiefships grew…

rashid-al-din-sinan.s: Rashid al-Din Sinan was the leader of the Nizari Ismailis in Syria from about 1162 to 1193, known to the crusaders as the Old Man of the Mountain. From the castle of Masyaf he made the Syrian Nizaris largely independent of Alamut and used targeted killings against enemies,…

ratan-singh-of-ratlam.s: Ratan Singh was a Rathore Rajput, a descendant of Raja Udai Singh of Marwar, who received Ratlam in Malwa from the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan in 1652 in reward for service. He founded the Ratlam state and was killed at the Battle of Dharmat in 1658, fighting in the imperial…

ratan-singh-of-charkhari.s: Ratan Singh was raja of Charkhari, a Bundela state of Bundelkhand. During the rebellion of 1857 he remained loyal to the British and was besieged in his fort by the rebel leader Tantia Tope.

ratu-kalinyamat.s: Ratu Kalinyamat was a daughter of Sultan Trenggana of Demak and ruler of Jepara on the north coast of Java after her husband Sultan Hadlirin was murdered in 1549. A powerful queen, she sent fleets against Portuguese Malacca in 1551 and 1574 and made Jepara a leading port.

raymond-iii-of-tripoli.s: Raymond III was count of Tripoli from 1152 and, through his wife Eschiva of Bures, prince of Galilee. He was regent of the Kingdom of Jerusalem twice and a rival of Guy of Lusignan.

raymond-iv-of-toulouse.s: Raymond of Saint-Gilles, count of Toulouse, was one of the leaders of the First Crusade. After the capture of Jerusalem he turned to the Lebanese coast and from 1102 besieged Tripoli from a castle he built on Mount Pilgrim.

rene-ii-duke-of-lorraine.s: René II was count of Vaudémont and from 1473 duke of Lorraine. He defeated and killed Charles the Bold of Burgundy before Nancy in 1477, ending Burgundian attempts to absorb Lorraine.

rhodri-the-great.s: Rhodri the Great, Rhodri Mawr, was king of Gwynedd from 844 who also gained Powys and Seisyllwg, ruling most of Wales. He won a notable victory over Viking raiders in 856.

rites-of-zhou.s: The Rites of Zhou is a Chinese classic describing an idealised government of the Western Zhou, with its officials arranged in six ministries. Probably compiled in the late Warring States period, it inspired reformers: Wang Mang tried to restore its institutions under the Xin…

river-bann.s: The River Bann is the longest river in Northern Ireland, flowing north through Lough Neagh to the Atlantic near Coleraine. In early medieval Ireland it marked the western limit of the Ulaid after the Uí Néill pushed them east, so that the Kingdom of Ulaid was confined to…

robert-clive.s: Robert Clive was an officer of the East India Company whose victories in the Carnatic wars checked French power in southern India. His victory at Plassey in 1757 over Siraj ud-Daulah, the nawab of Bengal, made the Company the real power in Bengal, and in 1765 he obtained the…

robert-fitzhamon.s: Robert Fitzhamon was a Norman baron who conquered the Welsh kingdom of Morgannwg around 1093, overthrowing its king Iestyn ap Gwrgant. He built a castle at Cardiff inside the old Roman fort and granted the fertile Vale of Glamorgan to his knights, founding the Lordship of…

rodolfo-graziani.s: Rodolfo Graziani was an Italian general who directed the brutal reconquest of Libya, deporting the nomads of Cyrenaica to concentration camps. He commanded on the southern front in the invasion of Ethiopia and became viceroy of Italian East Africa, where an attempt on his life…

roger-borsa.s: Roger Borsa was duke of Apulia and Calabria from 1085, succeeding his father Robert Guiscard in preference to his elder half-brother Bohemond, who was given Taranto. His rule was weakened by rebellious barons and he relied on his uncle Roger I of Sicily.

roger-williams.s: Roger Williams was an English Puritan minister banished from the Massachusetts Bay Colony in 1635 for his views on religious liberty and native land rights. In 1636 he founded Providence on land obtained from the Narragansett, and he secured a charter for Rhode Island, which…

ruaidri-ua-conchobair.s: Ruaidri Ua Conchobair was king of Connacht and the last high king of Ireland, recognised from 1166. The Anglo-Norman invasion that followed undermined his position, and by the Treaty of Windsor in 1175 he accepted Henry II's overlordship.

relic-of-the-tooth-of-the-buddha.n: Relic of the tooth of the Buddha
relic-of-the-tooth-of-the-buddha.s: The Relic of the tooth of the Buddha is a tooth venerated in Sri Lanka as a remnant of the Buddha, said to have been brought from Kalinga in the 4th century CE. Possession of the relic came to symbolise the right to rule, so successive Sinhalese capitals, from Anuradhapura to…

rhodesian-bush-war.s: The Rhodesian Bush War was the guerrilla war fought by the ZANU and ZAPU nationalist movements against the white minority government of Rhodesia. It intensified after 1972, with guerrillas operating from Zambia and Mozambique; tens of thousands died.

robert-rich-2nd-earl-of-warwick.s: Robert Rich, 2nd Earl of Warwick, was an English Puritan nobleman and colonial investor, a leading backer of the Providence Island Company, which settled Santa Catalina in 1630, and of other ventures in the Americas. During the English Civil War he commanded the…

rupert-of-germany.s: Rupert of the Palatinate was Elector Palatine and King of the Romans from 1400, when the electors deposed Wenceslaus, until his death in 1410. His authority was limited, and an expedition to Italy failed.

reunions.s: The Reunions were Louis XIV's policy of annexing territories on France's eastern border after the Treaty of Nijmegen of 1679. Special courts, the Chambers of Reunion, examined old feudal ties to claim lands in Alsace, Lorraine and elsewhere as dependencies of places already…

ranavalona-iii.s: Ranavalona III was the last monarch of the Merina kingdom of Madagascar, reigning from 1883 to 1897. Her prime minister and husband Rainilaiarivony governed while France imposed a protectorate in 1885 and invaded in 1895.

rabindranath-tagore.s: Rabindranath Tagore was a Bengali poet, novelist, composer and educator, the leading figure of the Bengal Renaissance. In 1913 he became the first non-European to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, for Gitanjali.

rachamalla-iv.s: Rachamalla IV was a king of the Western Ganga dynasty of southern Karnataka in the late 10th century. His minister and general Chavundaraya commissioned the colossal statue of Bahubali (Gommateshwara) at Shravanabelagola around 983, one of the greatest monuments of Jainism,…

raden-patah.s: Raden Patah was the founder and first sultan of Demak, the first Muslim sultanate of Java, in the late 15th century. Javanese tradition makes him a son of a Majapahit king and a Chinese mother.

rafi-ibn-makkan.s: Rafi ibn Makkan was an emir of the Banu Jami, an Arab family that ruled Gabès in southern Tunisia in the 12th century. Around 1117 he quarrelled with the Zirids of Mahdia over his merchant ship and appealed to Roger II of Sicily, an early step in the Norman intervention in…

rafic-hariri.s: Rafic Hariri was a Lebanese businessman who made his fortune in Saudi Arabia and served as prime minister of Lebanon in 1992–1998 and 2000–2004, leading the reconstruction of Beirut after the civil war. His assassination by a car bomb on 14 February 2005 set off mass protests,…

raghuji-i-bhonsle.s: Raghuji Bhonsle was a Maratha general who around 1739 established himself at Nagpur and founded the Bhonsle kingdom of Nagpur, absorbing the Gond kingdom of Deogarh. In the 1740s his armies raided Bengal repeatedly, and in 1751 the nawab Alivardi Khan ceded Orissa to him.

raghuji-ii-bhonsle.s: Raghuji II was the Bhonsle raja of Nagpur from 1788 to 1816. In the Second Anglo-Maratha War he joined Scindia against the British and was defeated at Assaye and Argaon in 1803.

raghunatha-nayak.s: Raghunatha Nayak was the most celebrated ruler of the Nayak kingdom of Thanjavur in the Kaveri delta. A loyal vassal of the Vijayanagara Empire, he fought for it in its succession war, notably at Toppur in 1616.

raghunatha-raya-thondaiman.s: Raghunatha Raya Thondaiman was the founder of the princely state of Pudukkottai in Tamil Nadu. A chief in the service of the Sethupathi of Ramnad, he established his own principality in 1686 between Thanjavur and Ramnad.

rahmon-nabiyev.s: Rahmon Nabiyev was first secretary of the Communist Party of the Tajik SSR from 1982 to 1985. Returning to power in 1991, he was elected the first president of independent Tajikistan, but rising conflict between his supporters and an Islamist-democratic opposition turned into…

rai-sahasi-ii.s: Rai Sahasi II was the last king of the Rai dynasty of Sindh, according to the Chach Nama. After his death, his Brahmin chamberlain Chach married his widow and seized the throne at Aror around 632, founding the Brahman dynasty that ruled Sindh until the Arab conquest of 711–712.

rai-singh-of-bikaner.s: Rai Singh was raja of Bikaner from 1571 to 1612 and one of the leading Rajput generals of the Mughal emperor Akbar, serving in Gujarat and the Deccan. He built the Junagarh fort at Bikaner between 1589 and 1594, and his alliance with the Mughals brought the desert kingdom…

raigam-bandara.s: Raigam Bandara, also called Pararajasinghe, was a son of King Vijayabahu VI of Kotte in Sri Lanka. After he and his brothers killed their father in 1521, the kingdom was divided, and he received the Raigama district south of Kotte.

rainulf-drengot.s: Rainulf Drengot was a Norman mercenary leader in southern Italy. In 1030 Duke Sergius IV of Naples granted him Aversa to guard the frontier against Capua, making him the first Norman to hold a lordship in Italy.

raja-hijau.s: Raja Hijau, the 'Green Queen', was ruler of Pattani on the Malay Peninsula from 1584 to 1616, the first of four queens who reigned in succession for about a century. Under her Pattani prospered as a port trading with Chinese, Japanese, Portuguese and Dutch merchants, and the…

raja-kecil.s: Raja Kecil was a Minangkabau-backed adventurer who claimed to be the posthumous son of Sultan Mahmud Shah II of Johor. In 1718 he seized the Johor throne, but Bugis forces drove him out in 1722.

raja-melewar.s: Raja Melewar was a prince of the Pagaruyung royal house of Minangkabau in Sumatra who was invited in 1773 by the chiefs of the Minangkabau settlements inland from Malacca to become their overlord. Installed at Seri Menanti as the first Yang di-Pertuan Besar, he founded the…

rajah-matanda.s: Rajah Matanda, born Ache, was a ruler of Maynila, the Muslim port kingdom on the site of Manila, with close ties to the Brunei court. As a young commander of a Bruneian fleet he met the survivors of Magellan's expedition in 1521.

rajah-of-sarawak.s: Rajah of Sarawak was the title of the Brooke family, the 'White Rajahs', who ruled Sarawak in northern Borneo from 1841 to 1946. The sultan of Brunei granted it to the English adventurer James Brooke for helping put down a revolt, and it passed to his nephew Charles and then…

rajah-salalila.s: Rajah Salalila is remembered in tradition as the first ruler of the Bruneian-allied dynasty of Maynila, set up around 1500 after Sultan Bolkiah of Brunei is said to have conquered the town. His line, which included Rajah Matanda and Rajah Sulayman, ruled the Muslim port until…

rajah-siagu.s: Rajah Siagu was the ruler of Butuan in northern Mindanao who, with Rajah Kolambu of Limasawa, met Ferdinand Magellan's expedition in March 1521. Antonio Pigafetta's account of the meeting describes the gold worn by these chiefs, and Siagu is said to have attended the first…

rajah-sulayman.s: Rajah Sulayman was a ruler of Maynila who shared power with his uncle Rajah Matanda in the 16th century. He resisted the Spanish, and after a clash in 1570 Martín de Goiti burned the town.

rajaraja-narendra.s: Rajaraja Narendra was a king of the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi in Andhra, closely allied by marriage with the Chola dynasty. He ruled from Rajamahendravaram (Rajahmundry), and under his patronage the poet Nannaya began the Telugu Mahabharata, the founding work of Telugu…

rajendra-narayan-singh-deo.s: Rajendra Narayan Singh Deo was the last ruling Maharaja of Patna, a princely state in western Orissa, which merged into Orissa in 1948. He then entered politics as a leader of the Ganatantra Parishad and the Swatantra Party, and served as Chief Minister of Orissa from 1967 to…

rakai-pikatan.s: Rakai Pikatan was a 9th-century king of Medang in Central Java, of the Sanjaya line. His marriage to Pramodhawardhani, daughter of the Sailendra king Samaratungga, joined the two royal houses, and the Sailendras lost their hold on Central Java.

ralph-gonsalves.s: Ralph Gonsalves is a politician of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, leader of the Unity Labour Party and prime minister from 2001 to 2025, the longest in the country's history. His governments built the Argyle International Airport and promoted regional cooperation, while the…

ram-baran-yadav.s: Ram Baran Yadav is a Nepali physician and Nepali Congress politician who became the first president of Nepal after the monarchy was abolished in 2008. He served until 2015, through the long drafting of a new federal constitution and the earthquake of that year.

ram-khamhaeng.s: Ram Khamhaeng was the third king of Sukhothai, reigning from about 1279 to 1298, under whom the Thai kingdom expanded widely. Tradition credits him with creating the Thai script, recorded in the Ram Khamhaeng inscription.

ram-shah.s: Ram Shah was king of Gorkha, a small hill kingdom among the Chaubise principalities of central Nepal, in the early 17th century. An early ruler of the Shah dynasty, he enlarged the kingdom and was remembered for laws on justice, debts and weights and measures, which gave…

rama-kulashekhara.s: Rama Kulashekhara was the last known ruler of the Chera Perumals of Makotai, the dynasty that ruled much of Kerala from Makotai (Kodungallur). His reign followed long wars with the Chola Empire.

ramadan-bey.s: Ramadan Bey was the Turkmen leader who founded the Ramadanid dynasty in Cilicia, in southern Anatolia. After the decline of the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia, his Üçok Turkmen settled the Cilician plain, and around 1352 the Mamluk Sultanate recognised him as emir of the region.

ramai-deva.s: Ramai Deva was, according to tradition, the Chauhan Rajput founder of the ruling dynasty of Patna in western Odisha in the mid-14th century. From Patnagarh he became overlord of the neighbouring hill chiefs, a group known as the Athara Garhjat, the eighteen forts.

ramchandra-pant-amatya.s: Ramchandra Pant Amatya was a Maratha statesman who served Shivaji and his successors as a minister. During the war with Aurangzeb in the 1690s, while Rajaram was besieged at Jinji, he directed the defence of the Maratha homeland.

ramiro-garces-of-viguera.s: Ramiro Garcés was the first king of Viguera, a small kingdom in La Rioja carved out of the Kingdom of Pamplona. A younger son of García Sánchez I, he received the lands around Viguera with a royal title from his brother Sancho II around 970.

ramiro-ii-of-leon.s: Ramiro II was king of León from 931 to 951. In 939 he defeated the caliph Abd al-Rahman III at the Battle of Simancas, one of the greatest Christian victories of the Reconquista, and pushed the frontier south to the Tormes.

ramiz-alia.s: Ramiz Alia was the communist leader of Albania who succeeded Enver Hoxha as first secretary of the Party of Labour in 1985. Facing economic crisis, student protests and mass flight abroad, he allowed opposition parties in December 1990.

ramon-castilla.s: Ramón Castilla was a Peruvian general and president (1845–1851 and 1855–1862) who brought stability after decades of caudillo wars. Using revenue from the guano boom he built railways and modernised the state, and in 1854 he abolished slavery and the tribute paid by indigenous…

ramon-herrera.s: Ramón Herrera was a general who served as president of the South Peruvian Republic in 1838–1839, one of the states of the Peru-Bolivian Confederation led by Andrés de Santa Cruz. He governed under Santa Cruz's supervision while Chilean and Peruvian forces fought the…

ramon-i-of-pallars-and-ribagorza.n: Ramon I of Pallars and Ribagorza
ramon-i-of-pallars-and-ribagorza.s: Ramon I was the first independent count of Pallars and Ribagorza in the Pyrenees of north-eastern Iberia. Around 872 he broke away from the counts of Toulouse and made the two mountain counties a hereditary lordship of his own.

ramon-llull.s: Ramon Llull was a philosopher, mystic and missionary from Majorca, born soon after the Aragonese conquest of the island. He wrote over 200 works in Catalan, Latin and Arabic, including the novel Blanquerna and the Ars Magna, a method for proving Christian truths to Muslims and…

ramon-muntaner.s: Ramon Muntaner was a Catalan soldier, administrator and chronicler. He served with the Catalan Company in Byzantium and Greece and governed the island of Jerba for the Crown of Sicily from about 1311 to 1315.

rana-kumbha.s: Rana Kumbha was the Sisodia ruler of Mewar from 1433 to 1468. He fought the sultans of Malwa and Gujarat and fortified his kingdom with many strongholds, above all Kumbhalgarh.

rana-sanga.s: Rana Sanga was the Sisodia ruler of Mewar from 1508 to 1528 and the leading Rajput king of his time. He defeated the sultans of Malwa, Gujarat and Delhi and built a wide coalition of Rajput clans.

ranajit-malla.s: Ranajit Malla was the last Malla king of Bhaktapur in the Kathmandu Valley, reigning from 1722 to 1769. He completed the Golden Gate of the royal palace in 1754 and was a patron of Newar music and drama.

ranieri-casali.s: Ranieri Casali was the head of a leading family of Cortona in Tuscany who made himself lord of the city in 1325. Cortona had been a self-governing commune, but under Ranieri and his descendants it became a hereditary lordship of the Casali.

ranoji-scindia.s: Ranoji Scindia was a Maratha commander and the founder of the Scindia dynasty of Gwalior. Rising in the service of Peshwa Baji Rao I, he received a share of the revenues of Malwa around 1731 and ruled from Ujjain.

ranulf-de-blondeville-6th-earl-of-cheste.n: Ranulf de Blondeville, 6th Earl of Chester
ranulf-de-blondeville-6th-earl-of-cheste.s: Ranulf de Blondeville, earl of Chester from 1181 to 1232, was one of the most powerful English barons of his age. He stayed loyal to King John in the baronial wars and helped secure the minority government of Henry III.

ranulf-de-gernon-4th-earl-of-chester.n: Ranulf de Gernon, 4th Earl of Chester
ranulf-de-gernon-4th-earl-of-chester.s: Ranulf de Gernon was earl of Chester from 1129 to 1153 and a major figure in the civil war between King Stephen and the Empress Matilda. Seeking to control Carlisle and the north-west, he seized Lincoln Castle and in 1141 helped capture Stephen at the Battle of Lincoln.

rao-bika.s: Rao Bika was a Rathore prince, a son of Rao Jodha of Marwar, who founded the kingdom and city of Bikaner. In 1465 he led followers north into the Jangladesh region of the Thar Desert and won lands from Jat and Bhati chiefs.

rao-chhatrasal-of-bundi.s: Rao Chhatrasal was the Hada Chauhan ruler of Bundi in Rajasthan from 1631 to 1658. A commander in Mughal service, he fought in the Deccan and the north-west.

rao-deva.s: Rao Deva was a chief of the Hada branch of the Chauhan Rajputs who founded the state of Bundi in Rajasthan. In 1342 he took the area from local Meena chiefs and made Bundi his capital.

rao-jodha.s: Rao Jodha was the Rathore ruler of Marwar who founded the city of Jodhpur in 1459. After recovering his family's capital of Mandore from Mewar, he built a new capital on a rocky hill nearby, with the great fort of Mehrangarh.

rao-maldeo.s: Rao Maldeo was the Rathore ruler of Marwar from 1532 to 1562, under whom Jodhpur became the strongest Rajput state in western India. He conquered much of the surrounding region, including Nagaur, Ajmer and Bikaner.

rao-surjan.s: Rao Surjan was the Hada ruler of Bundi who held the great fortress of Ranthambore. Besieged by Akbar, he surrendered it in 1569 on favourable terms and entered Mughal service, becoming a respected commander and governor.

rashid-bin-humaid-al-nuaimi-iii.n: Rashid bin Humaid Al Nuaimi III
rashid-bin-humaid-al-nuaimi-iii.s: Rashid bin Humaid Al Nuaimi III was ruler of Ajman, one of the Trucial States on the Gulf coast, from 1928 until his death in 1981. During his long reign Ajman remained under British protection and balanced against its larger neighbour Sharjah.

rashid-bin-majid-al-mualla.s: Rashid bin Majid Al Mualla was the founder of the Al Mualla ruling family of Umm al-Quwain on the Trucial Coast. In 1775 he established a fortified settlement on a sandy peninsula there, which became the seat of the sheikhdom.

rashid-bin-saeed-al-maktoum.s: Rashid bin Saeed Al Maktoum was ruler of Dubai from 1958 to 1990 and the main builder of the modern city. He dredged Dubai Creek, opened an airport in 1960 and used the oil revenue that followed the offshore discoveries of 1966 to build Port Rashid and the Jebel Ali port.

rashidi-kawawa.s: Rashidi Kawawa was a Tanzanian trade unionist and politician, a close ally of Julius Nyerere. When Nyerere resigned as prime minister of Tanganyika in January 1962, Kawawa succeeded him until the country became a republic in December.

ratna-malla.s: Ratna Malla was the first king of Kantipur (Kathmandu), one of the three Malla kingdoms of the Kathmandu Valley. A son of Yaksha Malla, he established himself at Kathmandu after his father's death and broke away from his brothers at Bhaktapur.

raul-castro.s: Raúl Castro is a Cuban revolutionary and the younger brother of Fidel Castro. He fought in the 26th of July Movement and commanded Cuba's armed forces for nearly fifty years.

ravi-sher-singh.s: Ravi Sher Singh was the last Raja of Kalsia, a small Sikh princely state in eastern Punjab whose lands lay around Chhachhrauli in today's Haryana. After Indian independence he acceded to India in 1947, and in 1948 Kalsia was merged into the Patiala and East Punjab States…

ravi-varma-kulasekhara.s: Ravi Varma Kulasekhara was a king of Venad in southern Kerala who ruled from Kollam from 1299 to 1314. Taking advantage of the decline of the Pandya kingdom after the raids of the Delhi Sultanate, he campaigned across southern India and was crowned at Kanchipuram.

rawal-jaisal.s: Rawal Jaisal was a Bhati Rajput ruler who founded the city and fort of Jaisalmer in 1156. Leaving the older capital of Lodurva, he built his stronghold on the Trikuta hill in the Thar Desert.

raya-malla.s: Raya Malla was the first king of the separate kingdom of Bhaktapur in the Kathmandu Valley. When his father Yaksha Malla died in 1482, the Malla realm was divided among his sons: Raya Malla kept Bhaktapur, the old capital in the east of the valley, while his brothers founded…

raymond-of-poitiers.s: Raymond of Poitiers was prince of Antioch from 1136 to 1149, a younger son of Duke William IX of Aquitaine who married the heiress Constance. In 1137 he had to accept the overlordship of the Byzantine emperor John II Komnenos.

raymond-vi-count-of-toulouse.s: Raymond VI was count of Toulouse from 1194 to 1222. Accused of protecting the Cathars, he was excommunicated, and the Albigensian Crusade from 1209 brought northern French armies under Simon de Montfort into his lands.

raymond-vii-count-of-toulouse.s: Raymond VII was count of Toulouse from 1222 to 1249 and the last of his line. After the Albigensian Crusade he made peace with the French crown by the Treaty of Paris of 1229, ceding the Comtat Venaissin to the Church and marrying his heiress Joan to Alphonse of Poitiers.

raymond-roger-trencavel.s: Raymond-Roger Trencavel was viscount of Carcassonne, Béziers and Albi. When the Albigensian Crusade began in 1209, crusaders sacked Béziers and besieged him in Carcassonne.

raza-ali-khan.s: Raza Ali Khan was the last ruling Nawab of Rampur, a Muslim princely state in Rohilkhand, reigning from 1930. He introduced administrative reforms and expanded the state's famous library of Persian and Arabic manuscripts.

red-hugh-odonnell.s: Red Hugh O'Donnell was lord of Tír Chonaill in north-west Ireland. Imprisoned by the English in Dublin Castle as a youth, he escaped in 1591 and became chief of the O'Donnells.

red-jacket.s: Red Jacket, or Sagoyewatha, was a Seneca orator and chief of the Wolf clan. Named for the red coat he wore as a British ally in the American Revolution, he became the leading Seneca spokesman in dealings with the United States, negotiating over land and defending Seneca…

red-shoe.s: Red Shoe, or Shulush Homa, was a Choctaw war leader of the 18th century who broke with the nation's French alliance and sought trade with the British. His faction's killing of French traders in 1746 provoked a civil war among the Choctaw.

reginald-johnston.s: Reginald Johnston was a Scottish colonial official and scholar of China. From 1919 to 1924 he was tutor to Puyi, the last Qing emperor, in the Forbidden City, and described this in Twilight in the Forbidden City.

reginar-duke-of-lorraine.s: Reginar Longneck was the leading noble of Lotharingia at the end of the 9th century. He held counties around the Meuse and Scheldt, including Hainaut, and lay abbacies such as Echternach, and was recognised as duke or margrave in Lotharingia.

reinhard-heydrich.s: Reinhard Heydrich was a senior SS officer, head of the Reich Security Main Office and one of the main architects of the Holocaust, who chaired the Wannsee Conference in January 1942. Appointed deputy Reich Protector of Bohemia and Moravia in 1941, he ruled the Czechs by terror.

rene-goulaine-de-laudonniere.s: René Goulaine de Laudonnière was a French Huguenot explorer who led the second French expedition to Florida. In 1564 he built Fort Caroline near the mouth of the St Johns River, the centre of French Florida.

rene-of-chalon.s: René of Chalon was prince of Orange and a leading noble of the Habsburg Netherlands, where he served Charles V as stadtholder of Holland, Zeeland and Utrecht. He inherited Orange from his uncle Philibert of Chalon.

resid-mehmed-pasha.s: Reşid Mehmed Pasha was an Ottoman general and grand vizier under Mahmud II. He restored central authority in the Balkans and Anatolia, taking Missolonghi in the Greek War of Independence and defeating Mustafa Pasha Bushati of Shkodër in 1831.

revestment-act-1765.s: The Revestment Act of 1765 was the law by which the British government bought the sovereign rights over the Isle of Man from the Duke and Duchess of Atholl for £70,000. Its aim was to stop smuggling through the island, which cost the Treasury heavily in lost customs duties.

rexhep-mitrovica.s: Rexhep Mitrovica was an Albanian politician from Kosovo who served as prime minister of Albania under German occupation from November 1943 to February 1944. A nationalist who had served in earlier Albanian governments, he supported keeping Kosovo within Albania.

reynald-of-sidon.s: Reynald of Sidon was lord of Sidon in the Kingdom of Jerusalem. He spoke Arabic, was learned in Arabic literature and was respected by Saladin.

rhydderch-hael.s: Rhydderch Hael was a Brittonic king of Alt Clut, the later kingdom of Strathclyde, in the late 6th century. He appears in Welsh tradition and in the lives of Columba and Kentigern, the patron saint of Glasgow, as a Christian ruler.

richard-blanshard.s: Richard Blanshard was an English barrister who became the first governor of the Colony of Vancouver Island in 1849. He found that real power lay with the Hudson's Bay Company, which controlled land and trade, and that there were few settlers to govern.

richard-og-de-burgh-2nd-earl-of-ulster.n: Richard Óg de Burgh, 2nd Earl of Ulster
richard-og-de-burgh-2nd-earl-of-ulster.s: Richard de Burgh, known as the Red Earl, was earl of Ulster and lord of Connacht, the most powerful Anglo-Norman lord in Ireland around 1300. He was overlord of the O'Neills, built castles such as Ballymote and Northburgh and fought for Edward I in Scotland.

richard-de-clare-2nd-earl-of-pembroke.n: Richard de Clare, 2nd Earl of Pembroke
richard-de-clare-2nd-earl-of-pembroke.s: Richard de Clare, known as Strongbow, was a Cambro-Norman lord who led the Anglo-Norman invasion of Ireland. Invited by the deposed king of Leinster, Diarmait Mac Murchada, he landed in 1170, took Waterford and Dublin and married Diarmait's daughter Aoife.

richard-i-of-capua.s: Richard I was a Norman leader of the Drengot family who became count of Aversa in 1049 and prince of Capua in 1058, after taking the city from its Lombard ruler. He was one of the Norman lords, with Robert Guiscard, who took over southern Italy, and he swore fealty to the…

richard-nicolls.s: Richard Nicolls was an English officer who in 1664 commanded the fleet that took New Amsterdam from the Dutch without a fight. Acting for James, Duke of York, he renamed the town and colony New York and served as its first English governor until 1668.

richard-southey.s: Richard Southey was a Cape Colony official who served as colonial secretary and then as lieutenant-governor of Griqualand West from 1873 to 1875, after Britain annexed the diamond fields around Kimberley. He struggled to govern the unruly mining camps and was recalled after…

richard-the-justiciar.s: Richard the Justiciar was count of Autun and the first duke of Burgundy. A brother of Boso of Provence, he gathered the counties of western Burgundy under his rule and defended them against the Vikings, defeating them at Saint-Florentin in 898.

rinchen-zangpo.s: Rinchen Zangpo was a Tibetan translator and teacher who led the revival of Buddhism in western Tibet. Sent to Kashmir by the kings of Guge, he translated many Sanskrit texts into Tibetan and brought back Kashmiri artists.

rio-tinto.s: The Río Tinto is a river in Huelva in south-western Spain, named for its red, acidic waters. The mines of its upper basin hold some of the world's richest deposits of copper, silver and gold and have been worked for about five thousand years.

robert-barclay.s: Robert Barclay was a Scottish Quaker theologian whose Apology for the True Christian Divinity became the classic statement of Quaker belief. In 1682 he was one of the 24 proprietors who bought East Jersey, and he was made its governor for life, though he never went to America…

robert-bradshaw.s: Robert Bradshaw was a trade unionist and politician from Saint Kitts who led the Labour Party that dominated the islands' politics from the 1950s. He served as a minister in the West Indies Federation, and from 1967 as premier of the Associated State of Saint…

robert-codrington.s: Robert Codrington was a British colonial administrator who served as administrator of North-Eastern Rhodesia for the British South Africa Company from 1898 to 1907, governing from Fort Jameson (now Chipata). He set up the territory's administration, introduced the hut tax and…

robert-coryndon.s: Robert Coryndon was a British colonial administrator who began as secretary to Cecil Rhodes. As the British South Africa Company's representative and administrator in North-Western Rhodesia from 1897 to 1907, he governed through the Lozi king Lewanika.

robert-townsend-farquhar.s: Sir Robert Townsend Farquhar was the first British governor of Mauritius, which Britain took from France in 1810. He governed from Port Louis until 1823, allowing the Franco-Mauritian planters to keep their law, language and religion.

robert-henry-clarence.s: Robert Henry Clarence was the last hereditary chief of the Mosquito Reserve on the Caribbean coast of Nicaragua. In 1894 Nicaraguan forces under José Santos Zelaya occupied Bluefields and incorporated the reserve as the department of Zelaya.

robert-hodgson-mosquito-shore.s: Robert Hodgson was a British officer sent from Jamaica to the Mosquito Coast in 1740, during the War of Jenkins' Ear, to win the Miskito as allies against Spain. He became the first British superintendent of the coast, and in 1749 a formal superintendency was established with…

robert-ii-de-la-marck.s: Robert II de la Marck was lord of Sedan and duke of Bouillon, known as the Great Boar of the Ardennes. He fortified Sedan and claimed sovereignty, owing allegiance to neither the French king nor the emperor.

robert-louis-stevenson.s: Robert Louis Stevenson was a Scottish novelist, author of Treasure Island and Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde. From 1888 he travelled in the Pacific and wrote about the Gilbertese king Tem Binoka of Abemama.

robert-menzies.s: Sir Robert Menzies was Australia's longest-serving prime minister, in office from 1939 to 1941 and from 1949 to 1966. He founded the Liberal Party in 1944.

robert-schuman.s: Robert Schuman was a French Christian Democratic politician who served as prime minister and foreign minister under the Fourth Republic. On 9 May 1950 he proposed pooling French and German coal and steel production, the Schuman Declaration, which led to the European Coal and…

robert-king-of-naples.s: Robert the Wise was Angevin king of Naples from 1309 to 1343. The leading champion of the Guelph cause in Italy, he opposed the emperor Henry VII and failed to recover Sicily from its Aragonese kings.

robert-wagner-gauleiter.s: Robert Wagner was the Nazi leader of Baden, who took control of the state government in March 1933 and served as its Reich governor. After the fall of France he also ran occupied Alsace, where he imposed Germanisation and conscription.

rock-of-cashel.s: The Rock of Cashel is a limestone outcrop in County Tipperary, Ireland, that was the seat of the kings of Munster from about the 4th century. In 1101 King Muirchertach Ua Briain gave it to the Church.

roger-of-lauria.s: Roger of Lauria was an admiral in the service of the Crown of Aragon and Sicily, regarded as one of the greatest naval commanders of the Middle Ages. During the War of the Sicilian Vespers he won a series of victories over the Angevin fleets, including the Gulf of Naples in 1284.

rognvald-eysteinsson.s: Rognvald Eysteinsson was earl of Møre on the west coast of Norway in the late 9th century. According to the sagas he was a close ally of Harald Fairhair, who granted him Orkney and Shetland, which he passed to his brother Sigurd.

rognvald-kali-kolsson.s: Rögnvald Kali Kolsson was earl of Orkney from about 1136 to 1158, a nephew of the murdered Earl Magnus. He won the earldom with Norwegian help and in 1137 began St Magnus Cathedral in Kirkwall in his uncle's honour.

roman-the-great.s: Roman Mstislavich, called the Great, was prince of Volhynia from 1170 and of Halych from 1199, uniting the two into the principality of Galicia-Volhynia. He fought the Lithuanians, Polovtsians and Poles and for a time dominated Kiev.

ronald-storrs.s: Sir Ronald Storrs was a British official who served as military and then civil governor of Jerusalem from 1917 to 1926, under the Occupied Enemy Territory Administration and the Mandate. He founded the Pro-Jerusalem Society and required buildings in the city to be faced with…

ronald-webster.s: Ronald Webster was the leader of the Anguillan revolution against rule from Saint Kitts. After islanders expelled the Kittitian police in 1967, he headed the island council and in 1969 proclaimed the Republic of Anguilla, which led to a British landing.

roosevelt-skerrit.s: Roosevelt Skerrit is a Dominican politician of the Dominica Labour Party who became prime minister in 2004, at 31 one of the youngest heads of government in the world. His long tenure has seen recovery from Hurricane Maria in 2017 and heavy reliance on a…

roque-lopez.s: Roque López was a Filipino revolutionary leader from Panay who served as president of the Federal State of the Visayas, formed in 1898 after Spanish forces at Iloilo surrendered. The federal state, with a council representing the islands, recognised the authority of Emilio…

rory-odonnell-1st-earl-of-tyrconnell.s: Rory O'Donnell was the younger brother of Red Hugh O'Donnell and succeeded him as chief of Tír Chonaill. After the Nine Years' War he submitted to the English crown and was made Earl of Tyrconnell in 1603.

rory-og-omore.s: Rory Óg O'More was an Irish chief of the O'Mores of Laois, whose lands had been confiscated and settled with English colonists in the 1550s as Queen's County. He led repeated raids and revolts against the settlers and the English administration, burning towns such as Naas in…

rostislav-mikhailovich.s: Rostislav Mikhailovich was a Rus prince, son of Michael of Chernigov, who briefly held Halych before losing it to Daniel of Galicia. He married a daughter of King Béla IV of Hungary and around 1247 received the banate of Macsó south of the Sava, along with Bosnian lands, which…

rostislav-i-of-kiev.s: Rostislav Mstislavich, a grandson of Vladimir Monomakh, was prince of Smolensk from 1127 and later Grand Prince of Kiev. He made Smolensk independent of Kiev and in 1136 established a separate bishopric there.

royal-proclamation-of-1763.s: The Royal Proclamation of 1763 was issued by George III after Britain gained France's North American territories in the Treaty of Paris. It created the provinces of Quebec, East Florida and West Florida and reserved the lands west of the Appalachians for Indigenous nations,…

ruben-um-nyobe.s: Ruben Um Nyobe was a Cameroonian nationalist and secretary-general of the Union of the Peoples of Cameroon, founded in 1948. He demanded independence and the reunification of French and British Cameroon, and presented the case at the United Nations.

rudd-concession.s: The Rudd Concession was a document signed in October 1888 by the Ndebele king Lobengula, granting exclusive mining rights in his lands to agents of Cecil Rhodes led by Charles Rudd. Lobengula later said he had been deceived about its terms.

rudolf-brun.s: Rudolf Brun was the first burgomaster of Zürich. In 1336 he led a revolt of craftsmen against the old council of merchant and knightly families and introduced a guild constitution, which he headed for life.

rudolf-duala-manga-bell.s: Rudolf Duala Manga Bell was king of the Bell people of Douala in German Kamerun. Educated in Germany, he led legal resistance to the colonial plan to expropriate Duala land along the river, petitioning the Reichstag.

rudolf-i-duke-of-saxe-wittenberg.s: Rudolf I was duke of Saxe-Wittenberg from 1298 to 1356. A close ally of the emperor Charles IV, he secured for his line the Saxon electoral vote and the office of imperial arch-marshal against the claims of the Saxe-Lauenburg branch.

rudolf-ii-of-burgundy.s: Rudolf II was king of Upper Burgundy from 912 to 937. Defeated by the Swabians at Winterthur in 919, he turned to Italy and was crowned king there in 922, but was driven out by Hugh of Arles.

rudolf-iv-duke-of-austria.s: Rudolf IV, called the Founder, was Habsburg duke of Austria from 1358 to 1365. He founded the University of Vienna in 1365, began rebuilding St Stephen's Cathedral and had the Privilegium Maius forged to claim the title of archduke.

rudra-pratap-singh.s: Rudra Pratap Singh was a Bundela Rajput chief who founded Orchha in Bundelkhand in 1531, on an island in the Betwa river, and made it his capital. The Bundelas had risen in the region after the decline of earlier powers.

ruganzu-ii-ndori.s: Ruganzu II Ndori was a mwami, or king, of Rwanda, remembered in royal tradition as the refounder of the kingdom in the 17th century after a period of invasion and disorder. Many legends and places in Rwanda are associated with him.

ruggero-settimo.s: Ruggero Settimo was a Sicilian admiral and politician who headed the government of independent Sicily during the revolution of 1848–1849. The Sicilian parliament deposed the Bourbons and offered the crown to Ferdinando, Duke of Genoa.

rukn-al-din-khurshah.s: Rukn al-Din Khurshah was the last Nizari Ismaili imam to rule from Alamut. He succeeded his father in 1255 just as the Mongol army of Hulagu invaded Iran.

rukn-al-din-sam.s: Rukn al-Din Sam was the founder of the dynasty of atabegs of Yazd in central Iran. The son of a Turkish officer named Langar, he was appointed by the Seljuk sultan around 1141 as atabeg, or guardian, to the heiresses of the Kakuyid rulers of Yazd.

rusa-ii.s: Rusa II was king of Urartu in the first half of the 7th century BCE. After the Assyrian defeat of Rusa I in 714 BCE, he restored the kingdom's strength and built new fortress cities, including Teishebaini (Karmir Blur) near modern Yerevan and Rusahinili near Lake Van.
