rutger-jan-schimmelpenninck.s: Rutger Jan Schimmelpenninck was a Dutch lawyer and statesman who served as ambassador to France and Britain. In 1805 Napoleon made him Grand Pensionary of the Batavian Republic with wide powers, and he introduced a national tax system and education reforms.

ryukyu-islands.s: The Ryukyu Islands are a chain of islands stretching south-west from Kyushu towards Taiwan, of which Okinawa is the largest. They were the home of the Ryukyu Kingdom, a trading state that paid tribute to China, until Japan annexed them in 1879.

ryuzoji-takanobu.s: Ryūzōji Takanobu was a Japanese warlord of the Sengoku period from Hizen in north-western Kyushu. A former monk, he overthrew his family's overlords, the Shōni, and became one of the three great powers of Kyushu, known for ruthlessness.

ralph-abercromby.s: Sir Ralph Abercromby was a Scottish general of the French Revolutionary Wars. In 1797 he led the British expedition that captured Trinidad from Spain, beginning British rule there.

rebellion-of-the-three-guards.s: The Rebellion of the Three Guards was a revolt early in the Western Zhou dynasty by three brothers of King Wu, Guan Shu, Cai Shu and Huo Shu, who had been set to watch the conquered Shang. Allied with the Shang prince Wu Geng, they rose against the regency of the Duke of Zhou,…

raqqada.s: Raqqada was a palace city near Kairouan in Tunisia, founded in 876 by the Aghlabid emir Ibrahim II as his residence. In 909 the Kutama army of the Fatimid movement took it, and in January 910 Abdallah al-Mahdi was proclaimed caliph there.

red-tower-alanya.s: The Red Tower is an octagonal defensive tower by the harbour of Alanya on Turkey's Mediterranean coast, built in 1226 by order of the Seljuk sultan Kayqubad I. About 33 metres high and built of red brick on a stone base, it guarded the shipyard and port that made Alanya the…

riez.s: Riez is a small town in the Alpes-de-Haute-Provence department of south-eastern France. In Roman times it was a colony and the chief town of the Reii, a people of the region, and from the 5th century until the French Revolution it was the seat of a bishopric.

runder-berg.s: The Runder Berg is a hill near Bad Urach in Baden-Württemberg, south-western Germany, the site of a fortified Alemannic hilltop settlement of the 4th and 5th centuries. Excavations from 1967 found evidence of an elite residence, metalworking and fine jewellery production.

reitia.s: Reitia was a goddess of the ancient Veneti of north-eastern Italy, known from votive inscriptions and offerings. Her main sanctuary at Baratella, near Este, has yielded inscribed bronze styluses, writing tablets and figurines, suggesting links with healing, childbirth and the…

roger-bernard-iii-of-foix.s: Roger-Bernard III was Count of Foix from 1265 to 1302 and, through marriage, Viscount of Castelbon. He clashed at times with the kings of France and Aragon, was imprisoned by both, and was also known as a troubadour poet.

roxana.s: Roxana was a Bactrian noblewoman, daughter of Oxyartes, whom Alexander the Great married in 327 BCE. She bore his posthumous son, Alexander IV, in 323 BCE, and mother and son became pawns in the wars of Alexander's successors.

rajaraja-i.s: Rajaraja I was emperor of the Chola Empire of southern India, reigning from 985 to 1014. He conquered the Pandya and Chera lands, northern Sri Lanka, where he took Anuradhapura in 993, and the Maldives, and he ended Western Ganga rule at Talakad.

ruwanwelisaya.s: The Ruwanwelisaya is a great stupa at Anuradhapura in Sri Lanka, begun by King Dutugemunu in the 2nd century BCE and completed under his brother Saddhatissa. Built to enshrine relics of the Buddha, it is one of the most venerated monuments of Sri Lankan Buddhism.

rezin.s: Rezin was the last king of Aram-Damascus, reigning in the mid-8th century BCE. He allied with Pekah of Israel against Ahaz of Judah in the Syro-Ephraimite War, prompting Ahaz to seek help from Tiglath-Pileser III of Assyria.

rezon.s: Rezon was, according to the Bible, a former officer of Hadadezer of Aram-Zobah who fled after David's victory over his master and seized Damascus in the 10th century BCE. He became king there and an adversary of Solomon, founding the kingdom of Aram-Damascus, which soon…

retogenes.s: Retogenes, called Caraunius, was a nobleman of Numantia in Hispania during the Roman siege of 134–133 BCE. According to Appian, he slipped through Scipio Aemilianus's siege lines with a few companions to seek help from neighbouring Arevacan towns.

raul-alfonsin.s: Raúl Alfonsín was an Argentine lawyer and Radical Civic Union politician who served as president from 1983 to 1989, the first elected after the military dictatorship. He set up a commission to investigate the disappeared and allowed the trial of the juntas in 1985.

robert-kocharyan.s: Robert Kocharyan is an Armenian politician who led the self-proclaimed Nagorno-Karabakh Republic and then served as president of Armenia from 1998 to 2008. He came to power after Levon Ter-Petrosyan's resignation and kept close ties with Russia.

ruben-i-prince-of-armenia.s: Ruben I was an Armenian lord who around 1080 established himself in the Taurus mountains of Cilicia as Byzantine power in the region collapsed. A follower of Gagik II, the last Bagratid king of Armenia, he founded the Rubenid dynasty, which later ruled the Armenian Kingdom of…

rubenid-dynasty.s: The Rubenid dynasty was an Armenian ruling family named after its founder Ruben I, who established a lordship in the Taurus mountains of Cilicia around 1080. His descendants extended their power over the Cilician plain, and in 1198 Leo I was crowned king, founding the Armenian…

roccamonfina.s: Roccamonfina is an extinct volcano in northern Campania, Italy, between the Garigliano and Volturno rivers, active from about 630,000 to 50,000 years ago. Its fertile slopes and caldera were home to the Aurunci and Sidicini in antiquity, and the area is now a regional park.

rhineland.s: The Rhineland is the loosely defined region of western Germany along the middle and lower Rhine, with cities such as Cologne, Bonn, Koblenz, Mainz and Düsseldorf. Fortified by Rome, it later held the great ecclesiastical electorates and many small states of the Holy Roman Empire.

ramathibodi-i.s: Ramathibodi I, known before his accession as U Thong, was the founder and first king of Ayutthaya, ruling from 1351 to 1369. Linked by family to the older centres of Lavo and Suphannaphum, he built his capital on an island where three rivers meet the Chao Phraya.

red-fort.s: The Red Fort is the walled palace complex of the Mughal emperors in Delhi, built of red sandstone for Shah Jahan between 1639 and 1648 as the centre of his new city of Shahjahanabad. After 1857 the British occupied it, and in 1945–1946 it was the scene of the trials of…

rokkaku-clan.s: The Rokkaku were a Japanese warrior clan, a branch of the Sasaki, who served as shugo governors of southern Ōmi province from the Kamakura period. From their mountain castle of Kannonji they dominated the region in the early 16th century.

raichur-doab.s: The Raichur Doab is the triangle of fertile land between the Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers in the Deccan of southern India, named after the fortified town of Raichur. From the 14th to the 16th century it was the chief prize in recurring wars between the Vijayanagara Empire…

raiyoli.s: Raiyoli is a village near Balasinor in Gujarat, India, known for one of the world's richest dinosaur fossil sites. Bones and thousands of fossil eggs from the Late Cretaceous were found there in 1981 during geological surveys, and the predatory dinosaur Rajasaurus was…

ragged-guard.s: The Ragged Guard was a Hungarian irregular paramilitary force active after the First World War, made up largely of former officers, students and nationalist volunteers. In August 1921, when western Hungary was due to be handed over to Austria, its units attacked the Austrian…

rabia.s: Rabi'a was a large confederation of Arab tribes, traditionally descended from Rabi'a ibn Nizar, which included the Bakr ibn Wa'il, Taghlib and Abd al-Qays. Before and after the rise of Islam its tribes lived in eastern Arabia and upper Mesopotamia, giving their name to the…

rihanna.s: Rihanna, born Robyn Rihanna Fenty in Saint Michael, Barbados, is a singer, businesswoman and one of the best-selling recording artists of all time. She rose to fame in the mid-2000s with hits such as Umbrella and later founded the Fenty Beauty cosmetics brand.

rajab.s: Rajab is the seventh month of the Islamic lunar calendar. It is one of the four sacred months in which fighting was traditionally forbidden, a custom inherited from pre-Islamic Arabia.

rabbi-akiva.s: Rabbi Akiva (Akiva ben Joseph) was one of the leading Jewish sages of the early 2nd century CE, whose systematic teaching of oral law laid foundations for the Mishnah. Rabbinic tradition says he hailed Simon bar Kokhba as the Messiah.

rasamanjari.s: The Rasamanjari ('bouquet of delight') is a Sanskrit poem by Bhanudatta that classifies types of lovers, heroes and heroines. It became a favourite subject of Indian court painting, and the illustrated series made at Basohli in the late 17th century, including a set signed by…

robert-moffat.s: Robert Moffat was a Scottish missionary of the London Missionary Society who worked in southern Africa from 1817 to 1870. From his mission at Kuruman among the Batlhaping he travelled widely, befriended the Ndebele king Mzilikazi and translated the whole Bible into Setswana.

rabia-khatun.s: Rabi'a Khatun was a sister of Saladin and a member of the Ayyubid family. She married Muzaffar al-Din Gökböri, ruler of Erbil, and after his death in 1233 lived in Damascus.

raman-skirmunt.s: Raman Skirmunt was a Belarusian landowner and politician, a member of the first Russian State Duma. In 1918 he briefly headed the government of the Belarusian Democratic Republic.

ramlila.s: Ramlila is a dramatic re-enactment of the life of the god Rama, based on the Ramayana and especially Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas, performed across northern India in the weeks around the Dussehra festival. Performances combine recitation, song, dance and dialogue and are staged…

ramnagar-ramlila.s: The Ramnagar Ramlila is a month-long performance of the Ramlila held each year at Ramnagar, across the Ganges from Varanasi, under the patronage of the Maharajas of Benares. Begun in the 19th century, it is staged in different parts of the town, which serve as fixed sets, and…

ramnagar-varanasi.s: Ramnagar is a town on the east bank of the Ganges opposite Varanasi in Uttar Pradesh, India. Its sandstone fort was built in the mid-18th century by Balwant Singh, Raja of Benares, and remained the residence of the Maharajas, part of it now a museum.

ram-mohan-roy.s: Ram Mohan Roy was a Bengali scholar and social reformer, often called the father of the Bengal Renaissance. He campaigned against sati, the burning of widows, which the British banned in Bengal in 1829, and argued for women's property rights and modern education.

raja-ganesha.s: Raja Ganesha was a Hindu landholder of northern Bengal who seized power in the Bengal Sultanate from the Ilyas Shahi dynasty around 1414. His son Jadu converted to Islam and ruled as Jalaluddin Muhammad Shah until 1433, with an interruption in which Ganesha himself returned to…

rhodope-mountains.s: The Rhodope Mountains are a range in south-eastern Europe, mostly in southern Bulgaria with their southern slopes in Greece. Wooded and rich in ores, they were home to Thracian peoples such as the Bessi and hold rock sanctuaries such as Perperikon; legend makes them the…

ratsimilaho.s: Ratsimilaho was the founder of the Betsimisaraka confederation on the east coast of Madagascar. The son of the English pirate Thomas White and a Malagasy princess, he united the northern coastal clans against the Tsikoa around 1712 and ruled as king from Fenoarivo until his…

ratnagiri-odisha.s: Ratnagiri is a Buddhist site in the Jajpur district of Odisha, India, part of the 'Diamond Triangle' with Lalitagiri and Udayagiri. From about the 5th to the 13th century it was a major monastery and a centre of Vajrayana Buddhism, flourishing under the Bhauma-Kara kings.

ratnagiri.s: Ratnagiri is a port town on the Konkan coast of Maharashtra, western India, and the headquarters of a district of the same name. The British exiled the last king of Burma, Thibaw, there after the annexation of Upper Burma in 1885; he lived in a palace in the town until his…

rohida-fort.s: Rohida, also called Vichitragad, is a hill fort in the Western Ghats near Bhor in the Pune district of Maharashtra, India. Shivaji took it in the 1650s, and it later formed part of the territory of the Pant Sachivs of Bhor, who held it until the end of princely rule.

river-thames.s: The River Thames is the longest river wholly in England, flowing about 346 km from the Cotswolds through Oxford and London to the North Sea. Since prehistoric times it has been a highway and a boundary, separating Celtic peoples and later Anglo-Saxon kingdoms such as Wessex…

rangin-mahal.s: The Rangin Mahal, or 'coloured palace', is a palace inside Bidar Fort in Karnataka, India, built in the 16th century under the Barid Shahi sultans, mainly Ali Barid Shah I. It is known for its carved wooden columns, coloured tilework and panels of mother-of-pearl inlaid in…

roman-von-ungern-sternberg.s: Roman von Ungern-Sternberg was a Baltic German nobleman and White Russian general in the Russian Civil War. His Asiatic Cavalry Division drove the Chinese out of Urga in February 1921 and restored the Bogd Khan, while he ruled Mongolia with notorious brutality.

ravahiny.s: Ravahiny was queen of the Sakalava kingdom of Boina in north-western Madagascar in the late 18th century. Under her rule Boina reached its height, its port of Mahajanga flourished in the Indian Ocean trade, and the kingdom held authority over much of western Madagascar.

river-mersey.s: The River Mersey is a river of north-west England that flows into the Irish Sea through a wide estuary at Liverpool. Its name means 'boundary river', and in the early Middle Ages it formed the frontier between Northumbria and Mercia.

river-tyne.s: The River Tyne is a river of north-east England, formed by the North and South Tyne near Hexham and flowing past Newcastle and Gateshead into the North Sea. Hadrian's Wall ran close to it, and in the Middle Ages it formed the northern limit of the bishop of Durham's palatinate.

rogier-van-der-weyden.s: Rogier van der Weyden was an Early Netherlandish painter, official painter of the city of Brussels from 1436. His emotionally intense works, such as the Descent from the Cross now in the Prado and the Last Judgement altarpiece for the Hospices de Beaune, were widely copied…

rukn-al-dawla.s: Rukn al-Dawla, born Hasan ibn Buya, was one of the three Buyid brothers who founded the dynasty's rule in Iran and Iraq. He took Ray and Isfahan and governed the central and northern Iranian lands until his death in 976, receiving his honorific, 'pillar of the state', from the…

rib-hadda.s: Rib-Hadda was king of Byblos in the mid-14th century BCE and the most prolific author among the Amarna letters, writing dozens of appeals to the Egyptian pharaohs Amenhotep III and Akhenaten. He complained of the advance of Abdi-Ashirta and Aziru of Amurru and of the Habiru,…

regolini-galassi-tomb.s: The Regolini-Galassi tomb is an Etruscan chamber tomb in the Sorbo necropolis of Caere (Cerveteri), found intact in 1836 by the priest Alessandro Regolini and General Vincenzo Galassi. Dating from about 675–650 BCE, it held gold jewellery, silver and bronze vessels and a…

richborough.s: Richborough, Roman Rutupiae, is a site near Sandwich in Kent, England, where the Roman army landed in the invasion of 43 CE. It became a major port and supply base, marked in the late 1st century by a huge monumental arch, and in the 3rd century a fort of the Saxon Shore.

rochester-kent.s: Rochester is a town in Kent, England, where the Roman road of Watling Street crossed the River Medway. An Iron Age settlement and then the Roman town of Durobrivae, it became in 604 the seat of England's second-oldest bishopric.

reconcavo.s: The Recôncavo is the fertile coastal region surrounding the Bay of All Saints in the Brazilian state of Bahia. From the 16th century it was covered with sugar plantations and tobacco farms worked by enslaved Africans, which made it one of the richest parts of colonial Brazil.

rondonia.s: Rondônia is a state in the Amazon region of western Brazil, bordering Bolivia, with its capital at Porto Velho. It was created as the federal Territory of Guaporé in 1943 from parts of Mato Grosso and Amazonas, renamed in 1956 after the explorer Cândido Rondon, and became a…

recife.s: Recife is the capital of the Brazilian state of Pernambuco, a port built on islands and peninsulas where several rivers meet the Atlantic. It grew as the harbour of Olinda and became the capital of Dutch Brazil after 1630, when Johan Maurits of Nassau rebuilt it; the first…

ruth-shady.s: Ruth Shady Solís is a Peruvian archaeologist who has led excavations at Caral in the Supe valley since 1994. Her radiocarbon dates showed that Caral was a large planned centre by about 2600 BCE, making the Caral-Supe civilisation one of the oldest in the world.

river-eden-cumbria.s: The River Eden is a river of north-west England that rises in the Pennines and flows north-west through Cumbria, past Appleby and Carlisle, into the Solway Firth. Its fertile valley was the home of the Carvetii in the Roman period and was later guarded by medieval castles…

reims.s: Reims is a city in Champagne, north-eastern France, the Durocortorum of the Remi and later capital of the Roman province of Belgica. Clovis was baptised there by Bishop Remigius around 500, and most French kings were crowned in its cathedral, a Gothic masterpiece and World…

revash.s: Revash is an archaeological site of the Chachapoya culture in the Amazonas region of northern Peru, with funerary buildings set into a cliff face. The small house-like tombs, built of stone and mud mortar and painted in red and cream, held collective burials.

ranthambore-fort.s: Ranthambore Fort is a hill fortress in Sawai Madhopur district of eastern Rajasthan, India, known in Sanskrit as Ranastambhapura. It was the seat of a Chauhan dynasty from the 1190s until Alauddin Khalji captured it from Hammira Deva in 1301, and later passed between the Delhi…

raja-rajeshwara-temple-vemulawada.s: The Raja Rajeshwara Temple at Vemulawada in Telangana, India, is a Shiva temple and one of the most visited pilgrimage centres of the state. The temple complex goes back to the Vemulavada Chalukyas of the 8th to 10th centuries, who supported both Jain and Shaiva shrines in…

rathwa.s: The Rathwa are an Adivasi community of eastern Gujarat, living mainly in Chhota Udaipur district and neighbouring parts of Madhya Pradesh, India. Mostly farmers in the forested hills, they are known for the Pithora paintings made on the walls of their houses to honour the…

ruijin.s: Ruijin is a county-level city in the hills of southern Jiangxi province, China, near the border with Fujian. In November 1931 a national congress of Chinese soviets there proclaimed the Chinese Soviet Republic, and Ruijin served as its capital, known as the "Red Capital",…

red-sticks.s: The Red Sticks were the traditionalist faction of the Creek (Muscogee) people who, inspired by prophets and by Tecumseh's call to resist American expansion, rose against the accommodationist Creek leadership and the United States in 1813. Their attack on Fort Mims widened the…

rajendra-chola-iii.s: Rajendra Chola III was the last king of the Chola dynasty, ruling from about 1246 to 1279. He tried to restore Chola power against the Kadava chief Kopperunchinga and the rising Pandyas, at times with Hoysala help, but was defeated by Jatavarman Sundara Pandya I.

river-feale.s: The River Feale rises in the Mullaghareirk Mountains near the borders of Cork and Limerick and flows north-west through north Kerry, past Listowel, to the Shannon estuary near Ballybunion, Ireland. Part of its course forms the border between counties Limerick and Kerry.

richard-clement-moody.s: Richard Clement Moody was a British officer of the Royal Engineers who served as the first governor of the Falkland Islands from 1841 to 1848. In 1858 he led the Columbia Detachment of Royal Engineers to the new colony of British Columbia, where as chief commissioner of lands…

ratu-sir-kamisese-mara.s: Ratu Sir Kamisese Mara was a Fijian high chief from the Lau Islands and leader of the Alliance Party. He became chief minister in 1967 and the country's first prime minister at independence in 1970, holding office until 1992 apart from a short break in 1987.

ratu-sir-lala-sukuna.s: Ratu Sir Lala Sukuna was a Fijian high chief, soldier and administrator, regarded as the leading Fijian statesman of the colonial period. Educated at Oxford, he served with the French Foreign Legion in the First World War.

robert-venables.s: Robert Venables was an English soldier who commanded the land forces of Oliver Cromwell's Western Design, with Admiral William Penn leading the fleet. After their attack on Santo Domingo failed in April 1655, they captured Jamaica from Spain in May 1655.

robert-f-stockton.s: Robert F. Stockton was a United States naval officer and politician.

richard-seddon.s: Richard Seddon was an English-born politician and the longest-serving prime minister of New Zealand, in office from 1893 until his death in 1906. Leading the Liberal government, he oversaw old-age pensions, compulsory labour arbitration and land reform.

robert-e-lee.s: Robert E. Lee was an American soldier who commanded the Confederate Army of Northern Virginia during the American Civil War.

rendel-constitution.s: The Rendel Constitution was the constitution introduced in Singapore in 1955 on the recommendations of a commission led by Sir George Rendel. It created a Legislative Assembly with a majority of elected members and a Council of Ministers led by a chief minister, while Britain…

red-river-war.s: The Red River War of 1874–1875 was a campaign of the United States Army against the Comanche, Kiowa, Southern Cheyenne and Arapaho on the southern Plains, in the Texas Panhandle. It began after attacks provoked by the destruction of the bison herds, and columns of troops…

rocca-paolina.s: The Rocca Paolina was a fortress built in Perugia from 1540 to 1543 for Pope Paul III, designed by Antonio da Sangallo the Younger, after papal troops crushed the city's Salt War. It was built over the houses of the Baglioni family and symbolised papal domination.

reggio-emilia.s: Reggio Emilia is a city in Emilia-Romagna, northern Italy, on the Via Emilia between Parma and Modena, founded by the Romans as Regium Lepidi. A medieval commune, it passed to the Este in 1409 and formed part of the Duchy of Modena and Reggio until 1859.

regulating-act-of-1773.s: The Regulating Act of 1773 was the first act of the British Parliament to regulate the East India Company's government in India. It created the post of governor-general of Bengal, first held by Warren Hastings, with a council of four and authority over Madras and Bombay, and…

richmond-virginia.s: Richmond is the capital of the US state of Virginia, on the James River. It was the capital of the Confederate States of America from 1861 to 1865 and its main industrial centre, with the Tredegar Iron Works.

rhine-confederation-act.s: The Rhine Confederation Act was a treaty signed in Paris on 12 July 1806 by sixteen German states, including Bavaria, Württemberg and Baden, which left the Holy Roman Empire and formed the Confederation of the Rhine under Napoleon's protection. Within weeks Emperor Francis II…

roger-casement.s: Roger Casement was an Irish-born British consul whose 1904 report on atrocities in the Congo Free State, and later on the Putumayo region of Peru, made him a leading humanitarian. Turning to Irish nationalism, he sought German help for an Irish rising, was arrested on landing…

romanesque-architecture.s: Romanesque architecture is the style of building that spread across western Europe from about 1000 to the late 12th century. It is marked by thick walls, round arches, barrel and groin vaults, massive piers and sculpted portals, and was used above all for churches and…

ratae-corieltauvorum.s: Ratae Corieltauvorum was the Roman town on the site of modern Leicester, England, and the capital of the civitas of the Corieltauvi. It grew from a late Iron Age settlement and a Roman fort into a planned town with a forum and basilica, public baths and town walls.

rance.s: The Rance is a river in Brittany, France, about 100 kilometres long, flowing north to the English Channel between Dinard and Saint-Malo. Its long estuary was the heartland of the Iron Age Coriosolites and an important route for medieval Breton trade.

reja-de-san-millan.s: The Reja de San Millán is a document of 1025 preserved by the monastery of San Millán de la Cogolla, listing the villages of Álava that owed the monastery a yearly tribute of iron. Naming some three hundred settlements grouped by district, it is the main early source for the…

robert-ii-count-of-artois.s: Robert II was count of Artois from his birth in 1250, the son of Robert I, who had been killed at al-Mansurah. A leading French commander, he served in southern Italy for his uncle Charles of Anjou, defeated the Flemings at Furnes in 1297 and led the French army at Courtrai in…

robert-iii-of-artois.s: Robert III of Artois was a French noble, grandson of Robert II, Count of Artois, who spent decades claiming the county against his aunt Mahaut. When his use of forged documents was exposed, he was banished in 1332 and fled to England, where he urged Edward III to claim the…

ramon-berenguer-i-count-of-barcelona.n: Ramon Berenguer I, Count of Barcelona
ramon-berenguer-i-count-of-barcelona.s: Ramon Berenguer I, called the Old, was count of Barcelona from 1035 to 1076. He imposed his authority on a rebellious nobility, collected tribute from the Muslim taifas and bought rights over Carcassonne and Razès, extending Barcelona's reach north of the Pyrenees.

renaud-de-dammartin.s: Renaud de Dammartin was count of Dammartin and, through his marriage to Countess Ida in 1191, count of Boulogne. Falling out with Philip II of France, he allied with King John of England and Emperor Otto IV and fought against Philip at Bouvines in 1214, where he was captured.

rodrigo-of-castile.s: Rodrigo was the first known count of Castile, governing from around 850 under Ordoño I of Asturias. He resettled the abandoned town of Amaya in 860 and defended the eastern frontier of Asturias against the Emirate of Córdoba and the Banu Qasi.

raymond-roger-of-foix.s: Raymond-Roger was count of Foix from 1188 to 1223. He joined the Third Crusade, and during the Albigensian Crusade he was one of the main opponents of Simon de Montfort, fighting at Muret in 1213, while his sister Esclarmonde was a leading Cathar perfect.

radbot-of-klettgau.s: Radbot (c. 985–1045) was a count in the Klettgau and the earliest securely known ancestor of the Habsburg dynasty.

reginarids.s: The Reginarids were a noble family of Lotharingia descended from Reginar Longneck (died 915), who held counties in Hainaut and the Hesbaye. In the 10th century they fought the East Frankish kings for power in Lotharingia and were repeatedly exiled.

richilde-countess-of-hainaut.s: Richilde (c. 1031–1086) was Countess of Hainaut, married first to Count Hermann of Mons and then, in 1051, to Baldwin VI of Flanders.

rheinfels-castle.s: Rheinfels Castle is a ruined castle above Sankt Goar on the left bank of the Middle Rhine, Germany, built in 1245 by Count Dieter V of Katzenelnbogen to collect Rhine tolls. It withstood a siege by the Rhenish League in 1255–1256, became the residence of Landgrave Philip II of…

riesling.s: Riesling is a white grape variety native to the Rhine region of Germany, prized for aromatic, high-acid wines ranging from dry to sweet. Its earliest known written record is a 1435 cellar account of Count John IV of Katzenelnbogen at Rüsselsheim.

rotrou-iii-count-of-perche.s: Rotrou III was Count of Perche from about 1100 to 1144 and a leading crusader. He took part in the First Crusade, then fought for Alfonso I of Aragon against the Almoravids in the Ebro valley, receiving the lordship of Tudela.

ramnulfids.s: The Ramnulfids were a Frankish noble family that held the county of Poitou from the 9th century and, from the 10th century, the duchy of Aquitaine. Named after Ramnulf I, count of Poitiers in the mid-9th century, the line included William IX, the first known troubadour, and…

ramon-berenguer-iv-count-of-provence.n: Ramon Berenguer IV, Count of Provence
ramon-berenguer-iv-count-of-provence.s: Ramon Berenguer IV was Count of Provence and Forcalquier from 1209 until 1245, the last of the Barcelona line in Provence. He strengthened comital government and married his four daughters into royal houses: Margaret to Louis IX of France, Eleanor to Henry III of England,…

roda-de-isabena.s: Roda de Isábena is a small hilltop village in the province of Huesca, Aragon, in the valley of the Isábena. In the 10th century the counts of Ribagorza made it the seat of a bishopric, and its Romanesque cathedral of San Vicente, among the oldest in Aragon, still stands.

rinteln.s: Rinteln is a town on the Weser in Lower Saxony, below the Nesselberg, where the lords of Schaumburg had their first castle. Count Ernst founded a university there in 1621, which lasted until 1810.

rudolstadt.s: Rudolstadt is a town on the Saale in Thuringia, residence of the counts and later princes of Schwarzburg-Rudolstadt from 1599 until 1918. Their baroque palace, the Heidecksburg, overlooks the town.

roger-i-of-sicily.s: Roger I was a Norman adventurer of the Hauteville family, youngest brother of Robert Guiscard, who conquered Sicily from its Muslim rulers. He crossed the Strait of Messina in 1061, took Palermo with Robert in 1072 and completed the conquest in 1091, ruling as Count of Sicily.

ribagorza.s: Ribagorza is a historic region of the central Pyrenees, along the Ésera, Isábena and Noguera Ribagorzana valleys, today divided between Aragon and Catalonia. An independent county from around 872, it was taken over by Sancho III of Navarre in the 1010s and passed to Aragon in…

raron.s: Raron is a village in the Upper Valais, Switzerland, on the Rhône below the Bietschhorn. In the Middle Ages it was the seat of the powerful lords of Raron, and it later gave its name to one of the seven tenths, the self-governing districts of the Valais republic.

raymondines.s: The Raymondines were the dynasty of the counts of Toulouse, named after the name Raymond borne by many of its members. Established in the 9th century, they built a great principality across Languedoc, Rouergue and Quercy and, through Raymond IV, founded the County of Tripoli…

robertians.s: The Robertians were a Frankish noble family named after Robert the Strong, who defended the lands between the Seine and Loire against the Vikings in the 860s. His sons Odo and Robert I became kings of West Francia, rivalling the Carolingians, and his descendant Hugh Capet took…

robert-of-rhuddlan.s: Robert of Rhuddlan was a Norman knight, cousin and lieutenant of Hugh d'Avranches, Earl of Chester. From his castle at Rhuddlan he conquered much of the north Welsh coast and claimed rule over Gwynedd, after he and Hugh captured its king, Gruffudd ap Cynan.

rosli-dhobi.s: Rosli Dhobi was a Sarawak nationalist of the anti-cession movement, which opposed the transfer of Sarawak from the Brooke rajahs to the British crown in 1946. In December 1949, aged 17, he stabbed Governor Duncan Stewart at Sibu, and he was hanged in 1950.

river-clyde.s: The River Clyde is a river in southern Scotland, about 170 km long, flowing north-west through Lanarkshire and Glasgow into the Firth of Clyde. Its valley was the heart of the British kingdom of Strathclyde, centred on Dumbarton Rock, and from the 18th century Glasgow's trade…

royal-greenland-trading-department.s: The Royal Greenland Trading Department (Kongelige Grønlandske Handel) was a Danish state enterprise founded in 1776 that held a monopoly on trade with Greenland. It ran the trading stations, supplied the settlements and bought seal products and fish, and for long periods also…

river-lea.s: The River Lea is a river in south-east England, about 68 km long, rising in Bedfordshire and flowing through Hertfordshire to join the Thames in east London. Around 886 the treaty between Alfred the Great and the Danish leader Guthrum used it as part of the boundary between…

river-great-ouse.s: The River Great Ouse is a river in eastern England, about 230 km long, flowing from Northamptonshire through Bedford, Huntingdon and Ely to the Wash at King's Lynn. The treaty of around 886 between Alfred the Great and Guthrum used it as part of the boundary between English…

river-dee-wales.s: The River Dee rises in Snowdonia and flows through Bala Lake, Llangollen and the English city of Chester before entering the Irish Sea through a broad estuary between the Wirral and Flintshire. For much of its course it forms or follows the border between England and Wales.

river-dee-aberdeenshire.s: The River Dee in north-east Scotland rises in the Cairngorm mountains and flows east for about 140 kilometres past Braemar and Balmoral to the North Sea at Aberdeen. Its valley, Deeside, has been a royal holiday area since Queen Victoria bought Balmoral in the 19th century.

royal-newfoundland-regiment.s: The Royal Newfoundland Regiment is an infantry regiment, now part of the Canadian Army reserve, raised as the Newfoundland Regiment in 1914 for the First World War. It fought at Gallipoli and on the Western Front and was nearly destroyed at Beaumont-Hamel on 1 July 1916.

rani-of-jhansi-regiment.s: The Rani of Jhansi Regiment was the women's regiment of the Indian National Army, formed in 1943 under Subhas Chandra Bose and commanded by Lakshmi Swaminathan, later Lakshmi Sahgal. Named after Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi, a leader of the rebellion of 1857, it recruited mainly…

richard-squires.s: Sir Richard Squires was Prime Minister of Newfoundland from 1919 to 1923 and from 1928 to 1932. His governments were dogged by allegations of corruption, and in April 1932, during the Great Depression, a crowd protesting against him stormed the Colonial Building in St John's.

robert-bond.s: Sir Robert Bond was Prime Minister of Newfoundland from 1900 to 1909. He negotiated a reciprocity treaty with the United States in 1902, which the US Senate blocked, and pressed Britain over French and American fishing rights on the island's coasts.

reichenau-island.s: Reichenau is an island in Lake Constance, in south-western Germany, joined to the mainland by a causeway. The Benedictine abbey founded there by the wandering bishop Pirmin in 724 became a major centre of learning, book painting and church building under the Carolingians and…

recklinghausen.s: Recklinghausen is a city in the Ruhr area of North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany. From the 13th century it was the centre of the Vest Recklinghausen, an outlying territory of the Electorate of Cologne, which passed to the Duke of Arenberg in 1803 and to Prussia in 1815.

robert-count-of-clermont.s: Robert of Clermont was the sixth son of King Louis IX of France and held the county of Clermont-en-Beauvaisis. Through his marriage in 1272 to Beatrice of Burgundy, heiress of the lordship of Bourbon, he founded the Capetian House of Bourbon, later the royal house of France.

rundale-palace.s: Rundāle Palace is a baroque palace in southern Latvia built from 1736 as the summer residence of Ernst Johann von Biron, Duke of Courland, to designs by Francesco Bartolomeo Rastrelli. Work stopped when Biron was exiled in 1740 and was completed in 1768 after his return, with…

ratchis.s: Ratchis was Duke of Friuli from 739 and King of the Lombards from 744 to 749. His conciliatory policy towards the Romans and the papacy angered the Lombard nobles, and he abdicated to become a monk at Monte Cassino, leaving the throne to his brother Aistulf.

reginald-i-count-of-guelders.s: Reginald I was Count of Guelders from 1271 to 1318. He claimed the Duchy of Limburg through his wife, but in the War of the Limburg Succession he and the Archbishop of Cologne were defeated by John I of Brabant at the Battle of Worringen in 1288, and he gave up his claim.

reginald-ii-duke-of-guelders.s: Reginald II, called the Black, was Count of Guelders from 1326 and its first duke from 1339, when Emperor Louis IV raised it to a duchy. He enlarged the territory and strengthened its finances through tolls on the Rhine.

roermond.s: Roermond is a city in the Dutch province of Limburg, where the Roer joins the Meuse. A chief town of the Duchy of Guelders, it became the capital of Upper Guelders and the seat of a bishopric in 1559, and it stayed with the Spanish Netherlands after the Dutch Revolt.

remonstrants.s: The Remonstrants are a Dutch Protestant movement that followed the teaching of Jacobus Arminius, who rejected strict Calvinist predestination. Named after their Remonstrance of 1610, they were condemned by the Synod of Dort in 1618–1619, and their preachers were exiled.

ricciarda-malaspina.s: Ricciarda Malaspina (1497–1553) was Marchioness of Massa and Lady of Carrara, heiress of the Malaspina lords of Massa. Her marriage in 1520 to Lorenzo Cybo, a nephew of Pope Leo X, brought the state to the Cybo family, and she governed it herself for long periods.

rinaldo-d-este-duke-of-modena.s: Rinaldo d'Este (1655–1737) was Duke of Modena and Reggio from 1695. A cardinal, he gave up his Church career to marry and continue the Este line, and in 1710 he bought the Duchy of Mirandola.

rheingau.s: The Rheingau is a region of Hesse, Germany, on the north bank of the Rhine between Wiesbaden and Lorch, where the river flows westward below the Taunus hills. Held for centuries by the archbishops of Mainz and later part of the Duchy of Nassau, it is one of Germany's oldest…

raciborz.s: Racibórz (German: Ratibor) is a town in the Silesian Voivodeship of southern Poland, on the upper Oder. From the late 12th century it was a seat of the Piast dukes of Upper Silesia and later the capital of the separate Duchy of Racibórz.

rawa-voivodeship.s: The Rawa Voivodeship was a province of the Kingdom of Poland and later the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, created in 1462 when the Masovian duchy of Rawa was incorporated into the Crown. Its seat was Rawa Mazowiecka, and it comprised the lands of Rawa, Sochaczew and Gostynin.

ramiro-de-lorqua.s: Ramiro de Lorqua was a Spanish captain in the service of Cesare Borgia, who made him governor of the newly conquered Romagna in 1501. He restored order with great harshness, and in December 1502 Cesare had him arrested and executed, displaying his body in the main square of…

rudolf-ii-holy-roman-emperor.s: Rudolf II was a Habsburg ruler, King of Hungary from 1572, King of Bohemia from 1575 and Holy Roman Emperor from 1576 to 1612. He moved his court to Prague, where he patronised artists and scholars such as Giuseppe Arcimboldo, Tycho Brahe and Johannes Kepler.

romhild.s: Römhild is a small town in the Hildburghausen district of southern Thuringia, Germany. Its collegiate church holds tombs of the counts of Henneberg, including bronze work from the Vischer workshop in Nuremberg.

radziwill-family.s: The Radziwiłł family was a magnate dynasty of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, prominent from the fifteenth century. Raised to princes of the Holy Roman Empire in the sixteenth century, its members held the highest offices of Lithuania and vast estates centred on Nesvizh and…

robert-the-strong.s: Robert the Strong was a Frankish count and margrave of Neustria under King Charles the Bald, charged with defending the lands between the Seine and the Loire against Vikings and Bretons. He was killed fighting them at Brissarthe in 866.

radulf-of-thuringia.s: Radulf was a Frankish nobleman whom King Dagobert I appointed Duke of Thuringia around 633 to defend the eastern frontier against the Slavs of Samo. After Dagobert's death he rebelled, and in 641 he defeated the army of the young King Sigebert III on the Unstrut.

raphael.s: Raphael (Raffaello Sanzio) was an Italian painter and architect of the High Renaissance, born in Urbino in 1483. After work in Perugia and Florence, he went to Rome in 1508, where he painted the frescoes of the Vatican Stanze, including The School of Athens, for Popes Julius…

rembrandt.s: Rembrandt van Rijn was a Dutch painter, draughtsman and etcher, born in Leiden, who worked in Amsterdam from the early 1630s. He is known for portraits, biblical scenes and a long series of self-portraits, and for his use of light and shadow, as in The Night Watch of 1642.

romsdal.s: Romsdal is a traditional district of western Norway around the Romsdalsfjord, in the county of Møre og Romsdal, with Molde and Åndalsnes as its main towns. It is known for steep mountains, including the Trollveggen rock wall.

rupert-of-salzburg.s: Rupert of Salzburg was a Frankish bishop and missionary, probably from Worms, who worked in Bavaria in the late 7th and early 8th centuries. Invited by Duke Theodo, he founded a church and the monastery of St Peter at the ruined Roman town of Iuvavum around 696, and the…

rupert-i-elector-palatine.s: Rupert I was count palatine of the Rhine, sole ruler from 1353, and the first of his line to hold the electoral dignity confirmed by the Golden Bull of 1356. He enlarged and consolidated the Palatinate on the Rhine and the Neckar and in 1386 founded the University of…

radbod-of-trier.s: Radbod was archbishop of Trier from 883 to 915, taking office soon after Vikings had sacked the city in 882. He rebuilt the church of Trier and was an adviser to the East Frankish and Lotharingian kings.

ruy-gonzalez-de-clavijo.s: Ruy González de Clavijo was a Castilian courtier sent by King Henry III of Castile as ambassador to Timur. Leaving Spain in 1403, he travelled through Constantinople, Trebizond, Erzincan and Persia and reached Samarkand in 1404.

rashidi-dynasty.s: The Rashidi dynasty, of the Shammar tribe, ruled the Emirate of Jabal Shammar in northern Arabia from its capital Ha'il between 1836 and 1921. Under Muhammad ibn Rashid it defeated the Al Saud and dominated central Arabia, with Ottoman support.

rif.s: The Rif is a mountainous region of northern Morocco along the Mediterranean coast, inhabited mainly by Riffian Berbers who speak Tarifit. It was the home of the early Islamic Emirate of Nekor and later of strongholds such as Chefchaouen.

redonda.s: Redonda is a small, uninhabited rocky island in the Caribbean, part of Antigua and Barbuda, lying between Montserrat and Nevis. Sighted by Columbus in 1493, it was mined for phosphate from guano in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

romanos-i-lekapenos.s: Romanos I Lekapenos was Byzantine emperor from 920 to 944. An admiral of humble origin, he became father-in-law and co-emperor of the young Constantine VII and governed in his place.

roy-welensky.s: Roy Welensky was a white Northern Rhodesian politician, born in Salisbury, who rose from railway worker and trade union leader to become prime minister of the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland from 1956 to 1963. A leading advocate of the federation, he defended white…

ross-scotland.s: Ross is a region of the northern Highlands of Scotland stretching from the Moray Firth to the west coast. It became an earldom in the early 13th century, and the claim of Donald, Lord of the Isles, to the earldom led to the Battle of Harlaw in 1411.

rhind-mathematical-papyrus.s: The Rhind Mathematical Papyrus is the largest surviving mathematical text from ancient Egypt, copied by the scribe Ahmose in the 33rd year of the Hyksos king Apepi from an original of the Twelfth Dynasty. It contains over eighty worked problems on fractions, arithmetic, areas,…

red-guards-finland.s: The Red Guards of Finland were armed militias of workers formed by the labour movement in 1917, after the Russian Revolution had removed the old order. In January 1918 they seized Helsinki and the industrial south, starting the Finnish Civil War against the White Guards.

red-vienna.s: Red Vienna was the period from 1919 to 1934 when the Social Democrats governed the city of Vienna. Funded by a new housing tax, the city built over 60,000 council flats in large estates such as the Karl-Marx-Hof, together with schools, clinics, baths and kindergartens.

ramon-matias-mella.s: Ramón Matías Mella was a Dominican patriot, counted with Juan Pablo Duarte and Francisco del Rosario Sánchez as one of the three founding fathers of the Dominican Republic. On 27 February 1844 he fired the shot that signalled the uprising against Haitian rule in Santo Domingo.

radegund.s: Radegund was a Thuringian princess captured by the Franks in 531 and married to the Merovingian king Chlothar I. She left him around 550, became a nun and founded the Abbey of the Holy Cross at Poitiers, which received a relic of the True Cross from Byzantium.

roquebrune-cap-martin.s: Roquebrune-Cap-Martin is a commune on the French Riviera between Monaco and Menton, centred on a hilltop village below a medieval castle. Long part of the Principality of Monaco, it joined Menton in breaking away in 1848 and was annexed by France in 1861.

rothschild-family.s: The Rothschild family is a Jewish banking dynasty founded by Mayer Amschel Rothschild in the Judengasse of Frankfurt in the late 18th century. His five sons set up banking houses in Frankfurt, London, Paris, Vienna and Naples, and in the 19th century the family became the…

riss.s: The Riss is a river in Upper Swabia, Baden-Württemberg, which flows north through Biberach to join the Danube. It gave its name to the Riss glaciation, one of the classic ice ages of the Alpine sequence.

rammelsberg.s: The Rammelsberg is a mountain in the Harz near Goslar in Lower Saxony, where silver, copper and lead ores were mined for over 1,000 years, from at least the 10th century until 1988. Its wealth drew the Salian emperors to build their palace at Goslar and made the town prosperous.

ravensburger.s: Ravensburger is a German toy and publishing company based in Ravensburg, Baden-Württemberg, founded in 1883 by Otto Robert Maier as a publisher of craft books and games. It is best known for its jigsaw puzzles and board games and remains one of Europe's leading games publishers.

regina-saskatchewan.s: Regina is the capital of the Canadian province of Saskatchewan. Founded in 1882 as the capital of the North-West Territories and named in honour of Queen Victoria, it became the headquarters of the North-West Mounted Police.

rothenburg-ob-der-tauber.s: Rothenburg ob der Tauber is a town in Franconia, Bavaria, above the Tauber valley, which grew below a Hohenstaufen castle and was a free imperial city from 1274 until 1802. Taken by Tilly's imperial army in 1631, it then declined, which preserved its walled medieval townscape,…

robert-bosch-gmbh.s: Robert Bosch GmbH is a German engineering company founded by Robert Bosch in Stuttgart in 1886 as a workshop for precision mechanics and electrical engineering. Its magneto ignition made it a leading supplier to the motor industry, and it became one of the world's largest…

riccardo-zanella.s: Riccardo Zanella was a politician from Fiume, now Rijeka, who led the Autonomist Party and became president of the Free State of Fiume after the elections of 1921. His government, which sought independence for the city, was overthrown by an Italian nationalist and Fascist coup…

rene-robert-cavelier-sieur-de-la-salle.n: René-Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle
rene-robert-cavelier-sieur-de-la-salle.s: René-Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle, was a French explorer in North America. After exploring the Great Lakes region, in 1682 he travelled down the Mississippi to the Gulf of Mexico and claimed its basin for France, naming it Louisiana after Louis XIV.

rosetta-stone.s: The Rosetta Stone is a granodiorite slab inscribed with a decree issued at Memphis in 196 BCE in the name of the Ptolemaic king Ptolemy V, written in Egyptian hieroglyphs, Demotic script and ancient Greek. French soldiers found it near Rashid (Rosetta) in the Nile delta in…

raja-dahir.s: Raja Dahir was the last Hindu king of Sindh, of the Brahman dynasty founded by his father Chach. Ruling from Aror in the late 7th and early 8th centuries, he faced the expedition sent by the Umayyad governor al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf after attacks on Arab ships near Debal.

rufisque.s: Rufisque is a city on the Cap-Vert peninsula east of Dakar in Senegal. A Portuguese and then French trading post, it became the main port for groundnut exports in the late 19th century and in 1880 one of the Four Communes, whose inhabitants held French citizenship.

redbad.s: Redbad, also Radbod, was king of the Frisians from about 680 until his death in 719. He fought the Frankish mayors of the palace, losing Dorestad and Utrecht to Pippin of Herstal around 690, but after Pippin's death in 714 he recovered them and defeated Charles Martel near…

river-shannon.s: The River Shannon is the longest river in Ireland, flowing about 360 kilometres from County Cavan south to an estuary on the Atlantic below Limerick. It separated Connacht from the provinces to the east and was a highway for Viking fleets, which founded Limerick on its estuary.

rourkela.s: Rourkela is an industrial city in Sundargarh district in northern Odisha, India. It grew around the Rourkela Steel Plant, the first integrated steel plant in India's public sector, built with West German collaboration from the mid-1950s and opened in 1959.

roatan.s: Roatán is the largest of the Bay Islands of Honduras, in the Caribbean Sea. In 1797 the British landed about 2,000 deported Garifuna there, from where they spread along the Central American coast.

rose-revolution.s: The Rose Revolution was the peaceful change of power in Georgia in November 2003. Protests against rigged parliamentary elections, led by Mikheil Saakashvili, Nino Burjanadze and Zurab Zhvania, culminated when demonstrators carrying roses entered parliament, and President…

rabaul.s: Rabaul is a town on Blanche Bay at the north-eastern tip of New Britain, Papua New Guinea. It became the capital of German New Guinea in 1910 and then of the Australian mandated Territory of New Guinea.

rusafa.s: Rusafa, called Sergiopolis in late antiquity, is a ruined city in the Syrian desert south of the Euphrates. It grew around the shrine of the soldier-martyr Saint Sergius, a major pilgrimage centre for Arab Christians, and the Ghassanid king al-Mundhir built an audience hall…

rabi-island.s: Rabi Island is a volcanic island in northern Fiji, east of Vanua Levu. It was bought in 1942 with Banaban phosphate royalties, and in 1945 the British resettled most of the people of Banaba there after the Japanese occupation of their home island.

raoul-wallenberg.s: Raoul Wallenberg was a Swedish diplomat who, as secretary at the Swedish legation in Budapest from July 1944, saved thousands of Hungarian Jews by issuing protective passports and sheltering them in buildings under Swedish protection. Detained by Soviet forces in January 1945,…

russification.s: Russification was the policy of spreading the Russian language, culture and administration among the non-Russian peoples of the Russian Empire and later the Soviet Union. It intensified under Alexander III from the 1880s, when Russian replaced German and other languages in the…

revolt-of-the-comuneros-paraguay.s: The Revolt of the Comuneros was a rising of Spanish settlers in the province of Paraguay between 1721 and 1735 against the authority of the viceroy of Peru and the Jesuit missions' control of Guaraní labour. Led at first by José de Antequera, who was executed in Lima in 1731,…

revolt-of-the-comuneros-new-granada.s: The Revolt of the Comuneros was a popular uprising in the Viceroyalty of New Granada in 1781, which began at Socorro against new taxes and royal monopolies imposed under the Bourbon reforms. Some 20,000 rebels marched on Bogotá and won concessions in the Capitulations of…

rionegro-convention.s: The Rionegro Convention was the constituent assembly that met at Rionegro, Antioquia, in 1863 after the Liberal victory in the Colombian civil war of 1860–1862. Dominated by radical Liberals, it adopted the Constitution of 1863, which created the United States of Colombia, a…

ryazan.s: Ryazan is a city in western Russia on the Oka river, south-east of Moscow. Called Pereyaslavl-Ryazansky until 1778, it replaced Old Ryazan, destroyed by the Mongols in 1237, as the seat of the princes of Ryazan in the fourteenth century.

rafael-antonio-gutierrez.s: Rafael Antonio Gutiérrez was a Salvadoran general and Liberal president of El Salvador from 1894 to 1898. He came to power through a revolt against Carlos Ezeta and joined Honduras and Nicaragua in the Greater Republic of Central America.

rastislav-of-moravia.s: Rastislav was ruler of Great Moravia from 846 to 870. Installed by the East Frankish king Louis the German, he soon asserted his independence, building strong fortresses and resisting Frankish attacks.

red-clouds-war.s: Red Cloud's War was a conflict of 1866–1868 between the United States and an alliance of Lakota, Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho led by the Oglala chief Red Cloud. It was fought over the Bozeman Trail and the army forts guarding it in the Powder River country of Wyoming and…

randsfjorden.s: Randsfjorden is Norway's fourth-largest lake, about 75 kilometres long, in the inland district of Oppland north-west of Oslo. The farming district of Hadeland lies around its southern end.

ronda.s: Ronda is a town in the mountains of Málaga province in Andalusia, Spain, built on either side of a deep gorge cut by the Guadalevín river. Under Muslim rule it was the centre of a taifa kingdom in the 11th century and later a frontier fortress of the Emirate of Granada.

razadarit.s: Razadarit was king of the Mon kingdom of Hanthawaddy in lower Burma from 1384 to 1421. He reunited the Mon-speaking provinces and fought the Forty Years' War against the Ava Kingdom of upper Burma, successfully defending his kingdom's independence.

richard-francis-burton.s: Sir Richard Francis Burton was a British explorer, soldier, linguist and writer. In 1855 he became the first European known to enter the walled city of Harar, and in 1857–1858 he and John Hanning Speke explored East Africa and reached Lake Tanganyika.

rajashekhara.s: Rajashekhara was a Sanskrit and Prakrit poet, dramatist and critic at the court of the Gurjara-Pratihara kings Mahendrapala I and Mahipala I at Kannauj. His works include the Prakrit play Karpuramanjari, the Sanskrit play Viddhasalabhanjika and the Kavyamimamsa, a treatise on…

robert-h-dyson-jr.s: Robert H. Dyson Jr. was an American archaeologist of the University of Pennsylvania who directed the Hasanlu Project in north-western Iran from 1956 to 1977.

raetia.s: Raetia was a Roman province in the central Alps and the Alpine foreland, covering parts of modern eastern Switzerland, southern Germany, western Austria and northern Italy. Conquered by Drusus and Tiberius in 15 BCE, it had its capital at Augusta Vindelicorum (Augsburg) and…

rijali.s: Rijali was an imam from Hitu on Ambon Island who wrote the Hikayat Tanah Hitu, a Malay chronicle of Hitu, in the mid-17th century. Opposed to Dutch rule, he spent years in exile, including at Makassar.

robben-island.s: Robben Island is a small island in Table Bay off Cape Town, South Africa. From the 17th century it was used to banish and imprison opponents of colonial rule, and under apartheid it held political prisoners, among them Nelson Mandela, who spent eighteen of his twenty-seven…

ralph-roys.s: Ralph L. Roys was an American scholar of the Yucatec Maya.

ramanuja.s: Ramanuja was a Hindu philosopher and theologian, the leading teacher of the Sri Vaishnava tradition of South India. His system of Vishishtadvaita, or qualified non-dualism, set out in commentaries such as the Sri Bhashya, taught devotion to Vishnu as the path to liberation.

red-terror-hungary.s: The Red Terror in Hungary was the campaign of repression carried out by the Hungarian Soviet Republic in 1919 against its real and supposed enemies. Revolutionary tribunals and armed squads, notably Tibor Szamuely's Lenin Boys, executed several hundred people, many after…

rugila.s: Rugila, also called Rua, was a king of the Huns in the 420s and 430s and the uncle of Attila and Bleda. He concentrated power among the Huns of the Danube plain, received tribute from the Eastern Roman Empire and supported the Roman general Aetius in the West.

razakars-hyderabad.s: The Razakars were a paramilitary force of the Majlis-e-Ittehadul Muslimeen in Hyderabad State, led by Qasim Razvi, that opposed the state's accession to India. In 1947-1948 they carried out attacks on Hindus and on opponents of the Nizam's regime.

risan.s: Risan is a small town on the Bay of Kotor in Montenegro and the oldest settlement on the bay. As Rhizon it was a royal seat of the Illyrian kingdom of the Ardiaei, where Queen Teuta took refuge from the Romans in 228 BCE.

rurikovo-gorodishche.s: Rurikovo Gorodishche is an archaeological site on the Volkhov river about two kilometres south of Novgorod in north-western Russia. Occupied from the 9th century, it was an early trading and princely centre with strong Scandinavian links, traditionally associated with Rurik.

rashad-al-alimi.s: Rashad al-Alimi is a Yemeni politician who has chaired the Presidential Leadership Council, the head of Yemen's internationally recognised government, since April 2022, when President Abdrabbuh Mansur Hadi transferred his powers to the council. A former interior minister and…

rio-pongo.s: The Rio Pongo is a river estuary on the coast of Guinea, north of Conakry, with many channels and creeks among mangrove swamps. In the 18th and 19th centuries it was a major centre of the Atlantic slave trade, where European, American and Euro-African traders bought captives…

rene-descartes.s: René Descartes was a French philosopher and mathematician who spent most of his working life in the Dutch Republic. His Discourse on the Method of 1637 and Meditations of 1641 founded modern rationalist philosophy with the principle 'I think, therefore I am', and he created…

regino-of-prum.s: Regino of Prüm was a Frankish monk, abbot of Prüm from 892 to 899 and later head of St. Martin's Abbey in Trier, where he died in 915.

ruhr.s: The Ruhr is an urban and industrial region in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany, named after the river Ruhr, a tributary of the Rhine that forms its southern edge. From the 19th century its coal mines and steelworks, in cities such as Essen, Dortmund, Duisburg and Bochum, made…

romani-people.s: The Romani people, or Roma, are an ethnic group whose ancestors left north-western India around a thousand years ago and reached Europe by the 14th century. Long subject to discrimination, enslavement in Wallachia and Moldavia, and expulsions, they were targeted for genocide…

rengat.s: Rengat is a town on the Indragiri River in Riau province, Sumatra, Indonesia, and the capital of Indragiri Hulu Regency. It became the seat of the Indragiri Sultanate in the later colonial period and was a Dutch administrative post.

riau.s: Riau is a province of Indonesia on the east coast of central Sumatra, with its capital at Pekanbaru. Crossed by the Siak, Kampar, Indragiri and Rokan rivers, it was home to Malay sultanates such as Siak and Indragiri.

riau-archipelago.s: The Riau Archipelago is a group of islands south of Singapore, including Batam, Bintan and the Lingga islands, now part of Indonesia's Riau Islands province. From the 16th century they were part of the Johor sultanate, and Bintan became a seat of its court and a centre of…

rasht.s: Rasht is the capital of Gilan province in northern Iran, near the Caspian Sea. It became the chief city of Gilan in the Safavid period and grew rich from the silk trade with Russia.

ruhollah-khomeini.s: Ruhollah Khomeini was an Iranian Shia cleric who led the Islamic Revolution of 1979 and became Supreme Leader of the Islamic Republic of Iran until his death. Exiled in 1964 for opposing the Shah, he preached from Iraq and France the doctrine of rule by the Islamic jurist.

robert-surcouf.s: Robert Surcouf was a French privateer and slave trader from Saint-Malo who operated in the Indian Ocean from Île de France, now Mauritius. During the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars he captured many British merchant ships, most famously the East Indiaman Kent in 1800.

rijeka.s: Rijeka, Italian Fiume, is a port city in Croatia on the Kvarner Gulf of the Adriatic. Hungary's main port under the Habsburgs, it was disputed between Italy and Yugoslavia after the First World War, occupied by D'Annunzio in 1919, made a free state in 1920 and annexed by Italy…

rameswaram.s: Rameswaram is a town on Pamban Island in the Gulf of Mannar, Tamil Nadu, India, facing Sri Lanka. It is one of the holiest Hindu pilgrimage centres, associated with Rama in the Ramayana, and its Ramanathaswamy Temple is famous for its long pillared corridors.

rajendra-singh-of-jaintia.s: Rajendra Singh was the last raja of the Jaintia kingdom in north-east India. After subjects of the British were seized in his territory and allegedly sacrificed, the East India Company annexed his lands in the Sylhet plains and then the Jaintia Hills in 1835, deposing him.

ranau.s: Ranau is a town in the hills of western Sabah, Malaysia, near Mount Kinabalu. In 1945 it was the destination of the Sandakan death marches, when Japanese guards forced Allied prisoners of war to march about 260 kilometres from Sandakan through jungle; of some 2,400 prisoners…

ramla.s: Ramla is a city in central Israel, founded in the early 8th century by the Umayyad prince Sulayman ibn Abd al-Malik. It became the capital of the province of Palestine under the Umayyads, Abbasids and Fatimids, and its White Mosque and underground cisterns survive.

rao-chunda.s: Rao Chunda was a Rathore chief of Marwar who took Mandore around 1395 and made it the capital of his growing realm. He extended Rathore power across much of the Marwar region, but was killed in fighting around Nagaur in the 1420s.

rao-siha.s: Rao Siha was the founder of the Rathore dynasty of Marwar, who according to tradition came from the Kannauj region and settled near Pali in western Rajasthan in the 13th century. A memorial stone at Bithu records his death in 1273.

rathore.s: The Rathores are a Rajput clan of north-western India, who ruled Marwar from Mandore and then Jodhpur from the 15th century. Branches founded the states of Bikaner, Kishangarh, Idar, Ratlam and many smaller principalities in Rajasthan, Gujarat and Malwa.

rudbar-of-alamut.s: Rudbar was a mountain district of northern Iran in the valley of the Shahrud and its tributary the Alamut river, in the highlands of Daylam. It was the centre of the Justanid kings, one of whom is said to have built the castle of Alamut in the 9th century.

raetian-limes.s: The Raetian Limes was the fortified frontier of the Roman province of Raetia, running about 166 kilometres from the Danube near Eining in Bavaria west to its junction with the Upper Germanic Limes. Built from the 2nd century, it was later reinforced with a stone wall.

rennyo.s: Rennyo was the eighth head of the Hongan-ji, the main temple of the True Pure Land school of Japanese Buddhism. Through preaching tours and simple pastoral letters he spread the faith among farmers and townspeople, above all in the Hokuriku region, turning a small sect into a…

ramappa-temple.s: The Ramappa Temple, or Rudreswara Temple, is a Shiva temple at Palampet in Telangana, India, built in 1213 by Recherla Rudra, a general of the Kakatiya king Ganapatideva. Named after its chief sculptor, it is famed for its finely carved basalt brackets and dancing figures and…

rudradeva-kakatiya.s: Rudradeva, also called Prataparudra I, was the Kakatiya ruler who made the dynasty independent of the Western Chalukya Empire. He declared sovereignty around 1163, recorded in an inscription at the Thousand Pillar Temple he built at Hanamkonda, and began laying out a new…

raipur.s: Raipur is a city in central India and the capital of the state of Chhattisgarh. It grew as the seat of a branch of the Kalachuris of Ratanpur in the 14th century, passed to the Bhonsles of Nagpur in the 18th century and became a district headquarters of the Central Provinces…

ratanpur.s: Ratanpur is a town in the Bilaspur district of Chhattisgarh, India. Founded in the 11th century by Ratnaraja I of the Kalachuri dynasty, it became the capital of the Kalachuris of Ratanpur, who ruled Dakshina Kosala for centuries, until the Marathas of Nagpur took it in 1741.

rajaram-i.s: Rajaram I was the younger son of Shivaji and Chhatrapati of the Maratha kingdom from 1689 to 1700. After his brother Sambhaji was captured and executed by the Mughals, he escaped south to Gingee, which held out against a long Mughal siege, while Maratha commanders fought on in…

rurik-dynasty.s: The Rurikids were the ruling dynasty of Kievan Rus' and its successor principalities, traditionally descended from Rurik, a Varangian said to have settled at Novgorod around 862. Princes of the family shared out the towns of Rus' among themselves, and its branches ruled Kyiv,…

russkaya-pravda.s: The Russkaya Pravda was the law code of Kievan Rus', whose earliest part is attributed to Yaroslav the Wise in the early 11th century, with additions by his sons and later by Vladimir Monomakh. It limited blood feud, set fines for injuries and killings according to social…

ruhinda.s: Ruhinda is the legendary founder of the Hinda dynasty, which ruled Ankole in Uganda and Karagwe and other Haya kingdoms in Tanzania. Traditions describe him as a son of Wamara, last ruler of the Chwezi of Kitara, who inherited the southern grazing lands and the royal drum…

ramiro-i-of-asturias.s: Ramiro I was king of Asturias from 842 to 850. He seized the throne after the death of Alfonso II, defeating a rival claimant, and faced revolts by nobles, a Viking raid on the Galician coast in 844, which he repelled, and warfare with the Emirate of Córdoba.

ramiro-i-of-aragon.s: Ramiro I was the first king of Aragon, ruling from 1035 to 1063. An illegitimate son of Sancho III of Navarre, he inherited the county of Aragon on his father's death and governed it as an independent realm, adding Sobrarbe and Ribagorza around 1045 after the death of his…

river-garry-perthshire.s: The River Garry is a river in Atholl, northern Perthshire, Scotland. It flows from Loch Garry near the Pass of Drumochter past Blair Atholl and through the Pass of Killiecrankie, scene of the Jacobite victory of 1689, before joining the River Tummel.

river-tummel.s: The River Tummel is a river of Perthshire, Scotland. It flows east from Loch Rannoch through Loch Tummel and past Pitlochry, where a hydroelectric dam forms Loch Faskally, and joins the River Tay near Ballinluig.

rajgir.s: Rajgir, ancient Rajagriha, is a town in Bihar, India, ringed by five hills. It was the first capital of the kingdom of Magadha under Bimbisara and Ajatashatru in the 6th and 5th centuries BCE, before the capital moved to Pataliputra.

richard-wagner.s: Richard Wagner was a German composer and theatre director whose operas, which he called music dramas, transformed European music. His works include Tristan und Isolde, Die Meistersinger von Nürnberg, the four-part Ring cycle and Parsifal.

river-tees.s: The River Tees is a river in northern England, flowing about 137 kilometres east from Cross Fell in the Pennines to the North Sea at Teesside. For much of its length it formed the historic boundary between County Durham and Yorkshire.

river-boyne.s: The River Boyne flows about 110 kilometres north-east through Kildare and Meath in Ireland to the Irish Sea at Drogheda. Its valley holds the Neolithic passage tombs of Newgrange, Knowth and Dowth, and the plain around it formed the early medieval kingdom of Brega.

river-liffey.s: The River Liffey rises in the Wicklow Mountains and flows in a wide loop through Kildare to Dublin Bay, dividing the city of Dublin into north and south. The Norse founded their settlement at Dublin near its mouth in the 9th century.

redon-abbey.s: Redon Abbey, the Benedictine abbey of Saint-Sauveur at Redon in eastern Brittany, was founded in 832 by the monk Conwoion with the support of Nominoe. It became the leading monastery of Carolingian Brittany, and its cartulary, recording hundreds of land grants, is a key source…

rhys-ap-tewdwr.s: Rhys ap Tewdwr was king of Deheubarth in south-west Wales from about 1078 to 1093. He held his throne against rivals partly through an arrangement with William the Conqueror, who came to St Davids in 1081.

rhys-ap-gruffydd.s: Rhys ap Gruffydd, known as the Lord Rhys, was ruler of Deheubarth in south-west Wales from 1155 to 1197. A grandson of Rhys ap Tewdwr, he recovered much of the kingdom from the Normans and reached an understanding with Henry II, who made him justiciar of south Wales.

river-usk.s: The River Usk rises on the Black Mountain in Wales and flows about 125 kilometres east and south past Brecon, Abergavenny and Usk to the Severn estuary at Newport. Its upper valley was the heart of the early medieval kingdom of Brycheiniog, and its lower course bounded the…

river-irfon.s: The River Irfon is a river in mid Wales that rises in the Cambrian Mountains and flows south-east through Llanwrtyd Wells to join the River Wye at Builth Wells. Its valley, with the middle Wye, formed the early medieval Welsh kingdom of Buellt, and Llywelyn ap Gruffudd was…

ronald-muwenda-mutebi-ii.s: Ronald Muwenda Mutebi II is the kabaka of Buganda, crowned in 1993 when President Yoweri Museveni restored Uganda's traditional kingdoms as cultural institutions. The son of Mutesa II, the last kabaka before the monarchies were abolished in 1967, he grew up largely in exile in…

ragnachar.s: Ragnachar was a Frankish king who ruled from Cambrai in the late 5th century, a relative of Clovis I. He supported Clovis against Syagrius at Soissons in 486, but around 509 Clovis bribed his followers, defeated him and killed him and his brother Richar.

river-dyfi.s: The River Dyfi, in English the Dovey, is a river of mid-Wales about 50 kilometres long that rises below Aran Fawddwy and flows south-west past Machynlleth to the sea at Aberdyfi. It has long been a boundary: in the Middle Ages between Gwynedd and Ceredigion, and today partly…

river-teifi.s: The River Teifi is a river of west Wales, about 120 kilometres long, that rises near the Teifi Pools in the Cambrian Mountains and flows past Tregaron, Lampeter and Cardigan to Cardigan Bay. For much of its course it forms the boundary between Ceredigion and Carmarthenshire,…

ripuarian-franks.s: The Ripuarian Franks were the Franks of the middle Rhine around Cologne, who took over the city as Roman rule collapsed in the mid-5th century. They had their own kings, the last being Sigibert the Lame and his son Chloderic, until Clovis I absorbed their kingdom around 509.

rathcroghan.s: Rathcroghan is a large complex of archaeological sites in County Roscommon, Ireland, identified with Cruachan, the ancient royal centre of Connacht. It includes burial mounds, ring-forts, linear earthworks and the cave of Oweynagat, and was used from the Neolithic onwards.

river-tamar.s: The River Tamar flows about 98 kilometres south from near the north coast of Cornwall to Plymouth Sound, forming most of the boundary between Cornwall and Devon. King Æthelstan is said to have fixed it as the border of the Cornish around 936, and it has long been seen as the…

royal-palaces-of-abomey.s: The Royal Palaces of Abomey are the complex of earthen palaces built by the kings of Dahomey at Abomey, in present-day Benin, from the 17th to the 19th century. Successive kings added their own palaces, decorated with painted bas-reliefs recording the kingdom's history and…

rime-movement.s: The Rimé movement was a non-sectarian movement in Tibetan Buddhism that arose in Kham in the 19th century. Led by Jamyang Khyentse Wangpo, Jamgön Kongtrul and others, it collected and preserved teachings from all schools, especially lineages at risk of being lost, and…

raika-dynasty.s: The Raika dynasty ruled the kingdom of Doti in far-western Nepal in the late medieval and early modern periods. Its kings traditionally claimed descent from the Katyuri rulers of Kumaon and governed from seats around Dipayal in the Seti valley.

river-deben.s: The River Deben is a river in Suffolk, England, flowing about 50 kilometres past Woodbridge to the North Sea at Felixstowe Ferry. Its valley was the heart of the early kingdom of East Anglia: the royal centre of Rendlesham and the ship burials of Sutton Hoo both lie beside it.

raedwald-of-east-anglia.s: Rædwald was king of East Anglia in the early 7th century and by 616 the most powerful king in southern England, named by Bede among the overlords of the English. In 616 he defeated and killed Æthelfrith of Northumbria at the River Idle, placing Edwin on the Northumbrian throne.

rendlesham.s: Rendlesham is a village in Suffolk, England, in the Deben valley. Bede names it as a royal residence of the East Anglian kings, and excavations since 2008 have revealed a large high-status settlement of the 6th to 8th centuries with a great hall, a few kilometres from the…

ross-on-wye.s: Ross-on-Wye is a market town in Herefordshire, England, on a sandstone cliff above the River Wye. It developed on an estate of the bishops of Hereford and is known for its 17th-century market hall.

robert-walpole.s: Sir Robert Walpole was a British Whig statesman who, as First Lord of the Treasury from 1721 to 1742, is regarded as the first prime minister of Great Britain. Under George I and George II he kept peace abroad, restored public finances after the South Sea Bubble and managed…

radnorshire.s: Radnorshire is a historic county of mid Wales, created in 1536 under the Laws in Wales Acts from marcher lordships between the upper Wye and the Severn valleys. It included the old districts of Gwrtheyrnion, Maelienydd and Elfael, with towns such as Rhayader, Presteigne and…

rhayader.s: Rhayader is a market town on the River Wye in mid Wales, in the historic county of Radnorshire, now Powys. It was the centre of the early medieval district of Gwrtheyrnion, and the Lord Rhys of Deheubarth built a castle there in 1177.

river-severn.s: The River Severn is the longest river in Great Britain, about 354 kilometres long, rising on Plynlimon in mid Wales and flowing through Shropshire and Worcestershire to the Bristol Channel. In the early Middle Ages its valley formed a frontier zone between the Welsh kingdoms…

river-wye.s: The River Wye rises on Plynlimon in mid Wales and flows about 215 kilometres through Rhayader, Builth Wells and Hereford to join the Severn estuary near Chepstow. Its lower course forms part of the border between Wales and England.

royal-netherlands-academy-of-arts-and-sc.n: Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences
royal-netherlands-academy-of-arts-and-sc.s: The Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences (KNAW) is the national learned society of the Netherlands, based in Amsterdam. It was founded in 1808 by Louis Bonaparte, king of Holland, as the Royal Institute of Sciences, Literature and Fine Arts, and was reorganised as an…

rashid-ali-al-gaylani.s: Rashid Ali al-Gaylani was an Iraqi nationalist politician who served several times as prime minister. In April 1941 he took power in a coup backed by four army officers known as the Golden Square and sought Axis support against Britain.

rostom-of-kartli.s: Rostom, born Khosrow Mirza, was king of Kartli in eastern Georgia from 1633 to 1658. A Muslim member of the Bagrationi royal house raised at the Safavid court, he was installed by Shah Safi and ruled as a loyal Persian vassal, bringing Persian customs to Tbilisi while…

rima-river.s: The Rima River is a river of north-western Nigeria that flows through Sokoto State and joins the Sokoto River near the city of Sokoto, whose waters then run south to the Niger. Its seasonally flooded valley, farmed and fished by the Kebbawa and other Hausa peoples, was the…

ramachandra-deva-i.s: Ramachandra Deva I was the founder of the Bhoi dynasty of Khurda in Odisha, eastern India. After the Karrani Afghans ended the independent Gajapati kingdom in 1568, he established himself at Khurda near Puri, and in 1592 Akbar's general Man Singh recognised him as raja under…

rama.s: Rama is a Hindu god, the seventh avatar of Vishnu and the hero of the Sanskrit epic Ramayana. In the epic he is a prince of Ayodhya in Kosala, of the Ikshvaku line, who is exiled to the forest, rescues his wife Sita from Ravana, the demon king of Lanka, and returns to rule in…

river-witham.s: The River Witham is a river of Lincolnshire in eastern England, flowing about 130 km from near Grantham through Lincoln to The Wash at Boston. It formed the southern boundary of the Anglo-Saxon kingdom of Lindsey, and its fenland valley has yielded many prehistoric finds, such…

rock-of-dunamase.s: The Rock of Dunamase is a limestone outcrop in County Laois, Ireland, crowned by the ruins of a castle. A fortress there was plundered by Vikings in 845 and later held by the kings of Leinster.

river-trent.s: The Trent is the third-longest river in England, nearly 300 kilometres long, flowing from the Staffordshire moorlands through the Midlands to join the Ouse and form the Humber estuary. Its upper valley was the heartland of the Anglo-Saxon kingdom of Mercia, and in the Middle…

red-ruthenia.s: Red Ruthenia is a historical region around Lviv and Przemyśl, in what is now south-eastern Poland and western Ukraine. Once part of Kievan Rus' and then of the principality of Galicia–Volhynia, it was conquered by Casimir III the Great of Poland from 1340 and became the…

river-conwy.s: The River Conwy is a river in north Wales, about 55 km long, that rises in the uplands of Snowdonia and flows north through the Conwy valley to the sea at the town of Conwy. It long formed a frontier between Gwynedd west of the river and the Perfeddwlad to the east, including…

robert-the-bruce.s: Robert the Bruce was King of Scotland as Robert I from 1306 to 1329. Seizing the throne after killing his rival John Comyn, he survived early defeats, waged a guerrilla war against the English and won a decisive victory over Edward II at Bannockburn in 1314.

rabdentse.s: Rabdentse was the second capital of the kingdom of Sikkim, in western Sikkim near Pelling, India. The second Chogyal, Tensung Namgyal, moved the court there from Yuksom in 1670, and it remained the capital until 1793, when invasions from Nepal forced a move to Tumlong.

rajasinha-i-of-sitawaka.s: Rajasinha I was king of Sitawaka in Sri Lanka from 1581 to 1593, son of Mayadunne. A renowned soldier, he conquered most of the west and the central highlands, including Kandy, and besieged the Portuguese in Colombo in 1587–1588 without success.

river-inny.s: The River Inny is a river in the Irish midlands that flows through Lough Sheelin and Lough Derravaragh and across Counties Westmeath and Longford into Lough Ree on the Shannon. In the early Middle Ages it divided the territory of Tethba into northern and southern parts.
